meta.title: Basic Banking Operations
meta.description: ELTP question bank covering the Business of Banking, Customer Service, Cash & Teller, Clearing, Treasury, Funds Transfer, E-Banking, Foreign Operations, and Fraud modules.

questionBank.q: Under BOFIA 2020 (as amended), which activity falls within the statutory definition of "banking business"?
opts: Underwriting corporate share issues for a client seeking a public listing
Receiving deposits and paying or collecting cheques
Managing a client's diversified real estate and equity portfolio for an annual fee
Providing tax advisory and international structuring services to large corporate clients
questionBank.exp: BOFIA 2020 (as amended) defines banking business around deposit-taking (current, savings, or similar accounts) and paying or collecting cheques drawn or paid in by customers. Options A, C, and D describe services banks may offer commercially but which fall outside the statutory core definition — they are non-banking financial or advisory activities, not the defining acts of banking business itself.

questionBank.q: A bank steps in to guarantee a customer's obligation to a third party so the transaction can proceed. Which role of banks does this illustrate?
opts: The payment role
The guarantor role
The agency role
The intermediation role
questionBank.exp: The guarantor role covers situations where the bank assures a third party that a customer's obligation will be met, enabling transactions that would otherwise stall on trust. The payment role concerns settling transactions on a customer's behalf; the agency role covers acting on instructions (e.g. standing orders); the intermediation role concerns channeling funds between savers and borrowers — none of these describe the bank assuming responsibility for another party's obligation.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the basic services banks provide to customers?
opts: Setting national interest rate policy for the entire banking sector
Brokerage services for buying and selling of stocks and shares
Auditing government revenue accounts on behalf of the Federal Ministry of Finance
Issuing national identity numbers to newly registered corporate entities
questionBank.exp: Brokerage services — buying and selling stocks and shares on a customer's behalf — is one of the basic services banks provide. Setting interest rate policy is a central bank function, auditing government accounts is a public-sector oversight function, and issuing national identity numbers is a government registration function — none are banking services rendered to customers.

questionBank.q: A bank notices that a growing share of its deposit base now sits in fixed-tenure accounts rather than current and savings accounts. Which trend affecting banks does this reflect?
opts: Deregulation of the banking sector by the Central Bank
An increasing interest-sensitive mix of funds
Consolidation and geographic expansion of banking operations
Service proliferation across newly opened branch networks
questionBank.exp: A shift in the balance between low-cost CASA (current/savings account) funds and higher-cost tenured deposits reflects the trend of an increasingly interest-sensitive funding mix, as depositors chase better returns. Deregulation concerns the regulatory environment, consolidation concerns bank mergers and market reach, and service proliferation concerns the range of products offered — none describe a shift in deposit composition.

questionBank.q: Which business group offers personalized financial and banking services traditionally reserved for high-net-worth individuals?
opts: Corporate Banking, for large companies and groups
Private Banking, for high-net-worth individuals
Retail Banking, for individual customers at smaller scale
Leasing, making assets available for rental payments
questionBank.exp: Private Banking is defined as personalized financial and banking services traditionally offered to a bank's wealthy, high-net-worth clients. Corporate Banking serves large companies or groups, Retail Banking serves individual customers at smaller scale, and Leasing makes assets available in exchange for rental payments — none target high-net-worth individuals specifically.

questionBank.q: Which support group is responsible for preparing periodic reports on management performance and controlling the budget against actual figures?
opts: Internal Control or Internal Audit
Financial Control
Credit Administration
Data Centre
questionBank.exp: Financial Control prepares periodic management performance reports and controls the budget versus actual financial figures. Internal Control/Audit checks compliance with Standard Operating Procedures rather than preparing budget reports, Credit Administration handles credit-related documentation, and the Data Centre processes data — none carry the budget-and-performance-reporting function.

questionBank.q: A customer deposits jewellery with a bank for safekeeping, and the bank does not take ownership of the items. Which banker-customer relationship does this describe?
opts: Debtor-Creditor, since deposited valuables become bank property
Bailor and Bailee, since ownership is not transferred
Principal and Agent, since the bank acts on instruction
Trustee and Beneficiary, since the bank administers the items
questionBank.exp: Safe custody of valuables, where items are transferred to the bank without transfer of ownership, establishes a Bailor (customer) and Bailee (bank) relationship. Debtor-Creditor applies to deposited money the bank owes back, Principal and Agent applies to instructed transactions like securities dealing, and Trustee and Beneficiary applies where the bank administers assets on another's behalf — none match safekeeping without ownership transfer.

questionBank.q: A bank wants to close a customer's current account that still has outstanding cheques in circulation. Following the principle established in Prosperity Ltd v Lloyds (1923), what must the bank do?
opts: Close the account immediately to prevent further cheque presentation
Give reasonable notice so outstanding cheques can be presented before closure
Notify the customer's employer before closing the account
Obtain a court order before closing any current account
questionBank.exp: Prosperity Ltd v Lloyds (1923) established that a bank will not cease doing business with a customer except upon reasonable notice, giving time for outstanding cheques to be presented before the account is closed. Immediate closure (A) directly contradicts this principle, and neither employer notification (C) nor a court order (D) feature in the ruling or in standard account-closure duties.

questionBank.q: A bank discloses a customer's account details to a regulator conducting a lawful investigation, without the customer's express consent. Which Tournier's case exception justifies this disclosure?
opts: Interest of the bank
Compulsion of law
Implied consent of the customer
Public duty
questionBank.exp: Compulsion of law covers disclosures a bank is legally required to make, such as responding to a lawful regulatory investigation, and applies without needing the customer's consent. Public duty covers disclosures made to protect the wider community rather than to comply with a legal requirement, interest of the bank covers disclosures protecting the bank's own position (e.g. recovering a debt), and implied consent requires circumstances suggesting the customer would agree — none fit a legally compelled disclosure to a regulator.

questionBank.q: A customer holds a credit balance in one account and an overdrawn balance in another account at the same bank, both in their own name. Which banker's right allows the bank to net these balances against each other?
opts: Right of Lien, over property held as loan security
Right of Set-off, netting balances in the same name
Right to Commission, for services already rendered
Right of Appropriation, which actually belongs to the customer
questionBank.exp: The Right of Set-off allows a bank to net a customer's credit balance against their overdrawn balance, provided both accounts are held in the same name and the same right. Right of Lien concerns retaining a customer's property in the course of extending credit rather than netting balances, Right to Commission concerns charging for services, and Right of Appropriation is actually a customer's right to direct payments, not a banker's right.

questionBank.q: A bank retains a customer's share certificates, lodged as security for a loan, until the loan is repaid — but the bank does not have this right over items the customer merely lodged for safe custody. Which principle, drawn from Foley v Hill (1848), explains why the right does not extend to safe-custody items?
opts: The Right of Lien requires the customer's written pledge, which safe-custody items lack
Safe-custody items sit under a Bailor-Bailee relationship, not the Debtor-Creditor relationship Lien attaches to
Safe-custody items are legally deemed to belong to a third party, not the customer
The CBN's tariff schedule excludes physical property from any banker's lien
questionBank.exp: Foley v Hill (1848) framed the ordinary bank-customer relationship as Debtor-Creditor, which is the relationship the Right of Lien attaches to when the bank extends credit. Safe-custody items sit under a separate Bailor-Bailee arrangement — the bank acts as bailee, not creditor — so lien does not extend to them. A written-pledge requirement, third-party ownership, and a CBN tariff exclusion are each plausible-sounding but incorrect bases; the actual distinction turns on which underlying relationship governs the property.

questionBank.q: What must a customer do when giving written payment instructions to their bank, in order to fulfil their duty as a customer?
opts: Countersign every instruction with a second authorized signatory
Exercise reasonable care in the instruction
Notify the bank's Internal Audit department before issuing the instruction
Submit instructions only through a registered agent recognized by the bank
questionBank.exp: A customer's duty is to exercise reasonable care in executing written orders, so as not to mislead the bank or facilitate forgery. Countersigning by a second signatory, notifying Internal Audit, or routing instructions through a registered agent are not duties described for customers generally — they may be internal bank controls or account-specific arrangements, not a customer's own legal duty.

questionBank.q: A customer who operates two accounts with the same bank makes a payment into the bank without specifying which account it should be credited to. Whose decision governs which account receives the payment?
opts: The bank decides, based on which account is more overdrawn
The customer decides, under the right of appropriation
The branch manager decides, based on internal policy
The CBN decides, through its consumer protection framework
questionBank.exp: The right of appropriation belongs to the customer: where a customer holds more than one account, they may direct which account a payment should be applied to, without duress from the bank. The bank, branch manager, or a regulator do not hold this decision-making right — it rests specifically with the customer making the payment.

questionBank.q: An employee at a company deposits a cheque made payable to their employer into their own personal account, and the bank processes it without query. Which act of negligence has the bank committed?
opts: Failure to obtain the employer's name during account opening
Diverting an employer's cheque into an employee's private account
Failure to see the original certificate of registration
Collecting a cheque inconsistent with the customer's status in life
questionBank.exp: Diverting into an employee's private account a cheque drawn by, or payable to, their employer is a specifically named act of negligence. The other listed negligence types describe different failures — omitting the employer's name at account opening, skipping a registration-certificate check, or collecting a cheque inconsistent with the customer's known status — none of which match a cheque made out to an employer being paid into a personal account.

questionBank.q: A bank collects a cheque crossed "account payee" for an account that does not belong to the named payee, without making any enquiry into the discrepancy. What has the bank failed to do?
opts: Verify the payee's original certificate of registration
Enquire before collecting a cheque payable to a different account
Obtain the payee's employer's name
Confirm the cheque was not previously dishonoured
questionBank.exp: Collecting a cheque crossed "account payee" for an account other than that of the named payee, without enquiry, is listed as its own distinct act of negligence — the crossing exists precisely to restrict payment to the named party, so collecting it elsewhere demands scrutiny. Certificate verification, obtaining employer details, and checking dishonour history are separate negligence categories tied to different scenarios, not this one.

questionBank.q: What is the primary purpose of the CBN's Consumer Protection Framework for banks?
opts: To set the statutory interest rate ceiling banks may charge borrowers
To engender public confidence and promote financial stability
To determine which banks may operate branches in rural areas
To approve proposed mergers and acquisitions between licensed banks
questionBank.exp: The Consumer Protection Framework was developed to engender public confidence and promote stability in the financial system, guaranteeing high service standards, market discipline, and fair treatment of customers. Setting interest rate ceilings, approving rural licensing, and approving mergers are separate CBN regulatory functions unrelated to the consumer protection mandate.

questionBank.q: Under the Responsible Business Conduct principle of the Consumer Protection Framework, what must a financial institution do before offering a product to a consumer?
opts: Obtain the NDIC's written approval before selling any product
Assess the consumer's capability and offer only suitable products
Require the consumer to complete a financial literacy course first
Publish the product's full terms in a national newspaper
questionBank.exp: Responsible Business Conduct requires institutions to assess consumers' financial capabilities and offer only suitable products or services based on their needs and capability, alongside high ethical standards. NDIC pre-approval per product, mandatory literacy courses, and newspaper publication are not requirements of this principle.

questionBank.q: Under the Disclosure and Transparency principle, what quality must information given to consumers about financial products have?
opts: It must be summarized to no more than one page
It must be accurate, timely, detailed, and clear
It must be approved by the customer's employer
It must be provided only upon written request
questionBank.exp: Disclosure and Transparency requires that information provided to consumers be accurate, timely, detailed, and clear, so they can make informed decisions. A one-page limit, employer approval, or a request-only basis are not conditions this principle imposes — the emphasis is on the quality and timeliness of disclosure, not its format or trigger.

questionBank.q: A bank employee accidentally exposes a customer's account details to an unauthorized third party, who then uses the information to defraud the account. Which principle of the Consumer Protection Framework has been breached?
opts: Fair Treatment, since the customer was treated with bias
Protection of Consumer Assets and Privacy
Consumer Financial Education, since the customer lacked awareness
Competition, since a rival bank benefited from the breach
questionBank.exp: Protection of Consumer Assets and Privacy requires that a consumer's financial and personal information be protected at all times and not released to a third party without consent, except as required by law. Fair Treatment concerns equitable service without bias, Consumer Financial Education concerns imparting financial knowledge, and Competition concerns market diversity of offerings — none address the unauthorized exposure of a customer's private information.

questionBank.q: What does the Complaints Handling and Redress principle require of a bank's complaints mechanism?
opts: That it resolves every complaint within 24 hours regardless of complexity
That it is affordable, fair, timely, transparent, accessible, and independent
That it is managed exclusively by the CBN
That it only accepts complaints submitted in writing
questionBank.exp: The Complaints Handling and Redress principle requires mechanisms that are affordable, fair, timely, transparent, accessible, and independent, to enhance overall consumer confidence. A fixed 24-hour resolution guarantee, exclusive CBN management, or a writing-only requirement are not conditions this principle sets — its focus is on the qualities the mechanism must have, not a rigid procedural rule.

questionBank.q: A bank's interest income from loans exceeds its interest expense on deposits for the period. What does this difference represent, as a source of bank income?
opts: Commission and Fees earned on services
Net Interest Margin
Advisory Fees earned on client transactions
Exchange Commission on currency conversions
questionBank.exp: Net Interest Margin is defined as interest income less interest expense — the surplus earned from the spread between what a bank earns on loans and what it pays on deposits. Commission and Fees, Advisory Fees, and Exchange Commission are all separate, non-interest income streams distinct from the interest-rate spread itself.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a component of the Commission and Fees income banks earn?
opts: Net Interest Margin, the spread between income and expense
Cost of Cheque Books
Loan loss provisioning set aside for bad debts
Statutory reserve requirement held with the Central Bank
questionBank.exp: Cost of Cheque Books is listed among the Commission and Fees a bank charges customers, alongside maintenance charges, exchange commission, advisory fees, and funds transfer charges. Net Interest Margin is a separate income category built on interest spread rather than fees, while loan loss provisioning and statutory reserve requirements are balance-sheet and regulatory items, not fee income.

questionBank.q: What broad shift in banking hall usage has resulted from the growth of online and mobile banking channels?
opts: An increase in foot traffic to local branches for routine transactions
Less foot traffic to branches, with more confusion when customers stop in for loans and financial support
Complete elimination of the physical banking hall
A shift of all lending activity to online-only channels
questionBank.exp: The growth of online banking has led to less foot traffic to local branches for routine transactions, while customers who do visit — often for loans or financial support — may find the reduced staff familiarity with in-branch processes more confusing. This falls short of eliminating the banking hall entirely (C), and lending has not moved to an online-only model (D); the banking hall remains the oldest banking channel still in active use.

questionBank.q: Given that all banks provide broadly homogeneous products, what approach is recommended for a bank to attract and retain customer loyalty?
opts: Reduce the range of products offered to simplify customer choice
Tie products and services to customer needs, with efficient, flexible, and approachable service delivery
Compete purely on lowering interest rates below regulatory minimums
Restrict services to only the bank's most profitable customer segment
questionBank.exp: Because banking products are largely homogeneous across the industry, differentiation comes from tying offerings to actual customer needs, providing a wide basket of services, and delivering them through efficient, flexible, approachable staff with a win-win mindset. Narrowing the product range, breaching regulatory rate minimums, or excluding customer segments run counter to the recommended differentiation approach.

questionBank.q: A bank exercises its Right of Set-off between a customer's current account and personal savings account, while the customer's items in the bank's safe-custody vault remain untouched. Why can the bank net the account balances but not touch the vaulted items under the same right?
opts: Because vaulted items are automatically insured and therefore exempt from set-off
Because Set-off applies to balances within a Debtor-Creditor relationship, while vaulted items sit under a separate Bailor-Bailee relationship the bank does not owe or hold as debt
Because Set-off only applies to accounts opened on the same calendar date
Because vaulted items must first be revalued by Financial Control before any right can attach
questionBank.exp: Set-off works by netting sums the bank owes the customer (Debtor-Creditor balances) against sums the customer owes the bank. Vaulted safe-custody items are held under a Bailor-Bailee arrangement — the bank never owes the customer their value as a debt, so there is nothing to net. Insurance status, account-opening dates, and Financial Control revaluation play no role in determining which right applies to which asset.

questionBank.q: A relationship manager gives a customer investment advice that leads to a financial loss, and the customer alleges the advice was negligent. Under which basis of the banker-customer relationship would such a claim most likely be assessed?
opts: Trustee and Beneficiary, since all advice implies a trust arrangement
Duty of care owed in tort, particularly where the bank gives investment advice
Principal and Agent, since the manager acted only on instruction
Bailor and Bailee, since advice is treated as a form of safekeeping
questionBank.exp: The manual specifically identifies a duty of care owed in tort as arising particularly where a bank gives investment advice — this is the basis on which negligent-advice claims would be assessed, separate from the routine Debtor-Creditor relationship. Trustee-Beneficiary requires an actual trust arrangement rather than advice alone, Principal-Agent describes acting on instruction rather than originating advice, and Bailor-Bailee applies to physical safekeeping, not advisory conduct.

questionBank.q: A walk-in customer wants to update the phone number linked to their account. Which unit is the first point of contact for this kind of request?
opts: Internal Control
The Customer Service Unit (CSU)
Credit Administration, which manages loan documentation
Treasury Operations, which manages money-market transactions
questionBank.exp: The CSU is the section set aside to manage customer needs and is the first point of contact for enquiries, account opening, record updates, complaints, and advert-driven walk-ins. Internal Control checks SOP compliance rather than serving customers directly, Credit Administration handles loan documentation, and Treasury Operations processes money-market transactions — none face the customer at first contact.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a function of the CSU Lobby Service Officer?
opts: Verifying signatories' international passports during account opening
Assisting with queue management to decongest the banking hall
Preparing the branch's periodic financial performance report
Approving deferrals on incomplete account documentation
questionBank.exp: Queue management to decongest the banking hall is a named Lobby Service Officer function, alongside welcoming customers and directing them to service points. Passport verification during account opening sits with account-opening documentation checks, financial performance reporting sits with Financial Control, and approving deferrals is reserved for designated senior staff — none are Lobby Service Officer duties.

questionBank.q: A CSU staff member ensures unissued cheque booklets are kept in fireproof cabinets and that stamps and customer files are secured before closing. Under the CSU's three functional classifications, which one covers this?
opts: Products and Services Management Function
Security Function
Client Information Services
Complaints Resolution Function
questionBank.exp: The Security Function covers safeguarding cheque booklets, stamps, and customer files, and maintaining confidentiality of customer data. Products and Services Management concerns knowing and discussing the bank's offerings, Client Information Services concerns enquiries and record maintenance, and "Complaints Resolution Function" is not one of the three named classifications at all — complaints handling sits elsewhere in the CSU's broad functions.

questionBank.q: A customer asks their bank to issue a reference letter on their behalf to support a business application. Which CSU functional classification handles this request?
opts: Security Function
Client Information Services
Products and Services Management Function
Treasury Function
questionBank.exp: Issuance of reference letters on behalf of clients is listed under Client Information Services, alongside status enquiries and database maintenance. Security Function covers physical safeguarding of documents rather than issuing them, Products and Services Management concerns discussing the bank's offerings, and there is no Treasury Function within the CSU's classification scheme.

questionBank.q: A customer wants to hold funds in US Dollars rather than Naira. Which product listed among the bank's offerings would meet this need?
opts: Call Deposit Account, for short-notice fixed funds
Foreign Currency (Domiciliary) Account
Ordinary Savings Account, for routine Naira savings
Non-Interest Bearing Current Account, for transactional Naira use
questionBank.exp: Foreign Currency Accounts, also called Domiciliary Accounts, are the product listed for holding funds in currencies other than Naira. Call Deposit and Savings accounts are Naira-denominated deposit products, and the Non-Interest Bearing Current Account is a Naira transactional account — none serve a foreign-currency holding need.

questionBank.q: A church appoints the bank to hold and administer funds on behalf of its members under a formal arrangement. Which account category fits this relationship?
opts: Investment Account, for deploying funds toward returns
Trustee Account
Partnership Account, for unincorporated business partners
External Account, under a separate classification entirely
questionBank.exp: A Trustee Account is the category listed for arrangements where the bank, or a named party, administers funds on behalf of others under a fiduciary duty. Investment Accounts concern deploying funds for returns, Partnership Accounts serve unincorporated business partners, and External Accounts serve a different classification entirely — none capture a fiduciary administration arrangement.

questionBank.q: A corporate customer applies to open a current account. As part of the account opening procedure, what must the bank do regarding the applicant's registration status?
opts: Accept the applicant's self-declared registration status without further check
Search CAC, and check CRMS and at least two Credit Bureaus
Rely solely on the applicant's Tax Identification Number as proof of registration
Wait for the customer's first transaction before verifying registration
questionBank.exp: The account opening procedure requires a search at the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), plus checks against the CBN Credit Risk Management System (CRMS) and at least two Credit Bureaus, for corporate accounts. Accepting a self-declaration, relying on the TIN alone, or deferring verification until after the first transaction all fall short of this multi-source verification requirement.

questionBank.q: Which document is specifically required for opening an Individual Current Account but is not listed among the requirements for a Savings Account?
opts: Two Passport Photographs of the signatory
Signature Mandate Instruction
Utility Bill showing the applicant's address
Identification of the Signatory
questionBank.exp: A Signature Mandate Instruction is listed specifically under Individual Current Account documentation and is not among the Savings Account requirements. Passport photographs, a utility bill, and signatory identification are required for both account types, so they don't distinguish the two.

questionBank.q: What additional requirement applies to a Joint Account that does not apply to a standard Individual Current Account, even though both share the same base documentation?
opts: A separate Tax Identification Number for each account holder
A mandate specifying how the joint account is to be operated
A Board Resolution authorizing the account's opening
A certificate of incorporation for each account holder
questionBank.exp: For joint accounts, the documentation matches a current account, but a mandate governing how the account is to be operated must additionally be taken. A separate TIN per holder, a Board Resolution, and a certificate of incorporation are corporate-account requirements, not something added for joint individual accounts.

questionBank.q: An NGO and a social club both apply to open accounts. Both submit identification for their signatories, but their supporting constitutional documents differ. What does the NGO submit that the club does not?
opts: A copy of Form 2 for registration of business name
A Trust Deed and Resolution of Trustees appointing signatories
Two completed reference forms from independent sources
A copy of the Constitution governing the association
questionBank.exp: NGO documentation specifically requires a copy of the Trust Deed and a Resolution of Trustees appointing signatories, reflecting its fiduciary structure. Form 2 for business name registration and a copy of the Constitution are club/association-specific requirements instead, while reference forms are common to both — they don't distinguish an NGO's documentation from a club's.

questionBank.q: A bank grants a deferral on a corporate customer's CO7 document while other checks are completed. What restriction applies to this specific deferral?
opts: The deferral may run indefinitely once approved by a senior officer
The deferral is capped at 30 days, with no cheque book issued
The deferral automatically converts to a documentation waiver after 90 days
The deferral requires the customer to open a separate account as security while checks continue
questionBank.exp: A CO7 deferral is capped at 30 days, and no cheque book may be issued while the deferral is in effect. An indefinite deferral, automatic conversion to a waiver, or a requirement to open a second account are not features of this rule — the two firm constraints are the time cap and the cheque-book restriction.

questionBank.q: A branch wants to defer a required document for a Public Sector account applicant. Who is authorized to approve this specific deferral?
opts: Any designated senior staff member, as with other account categories
Only very senior executive staff
The Customer Service Unit supervisor on duty
The Lobby Service Officer who first attended to the applicant
questionBank.exp: Deferrals for Public Sector accounts are restricted to only very senior executive staff, a tighter standard than the general rule allowing designated senior staff to approve deferrals for other account categories. A CSU supervisor or Lobby Service Officer sits well below this authorization threshold.

questionBank.q: A branch manager considers waiving a corporate applicant's Certificate of Incorporation to speed up account opening, since other documents look satisfactory. Is this permissible under the account opening guiding policies?
opts: Yes, provided the applicant signs an indemnity
No — statutory documents such as the Certificate of Incorporation cannot be waived
Yes, if Management grants a waiver for any non-vital document
No, unless the CBN issues a specific exemption letter
questionBank.exp: The guiding policies explicitly state that statutory documents — including the Certificate of Incorporation and client identification (KYC/KYCB) — cannot be waived, unlike certain non-regulatory documents which may be deferred for 30–90 days. An indemnity signature, a general Management waiver, or a CBN exemption letter don't feature as routes around this specific prohibition.

questionBank.q: A customer's current account attracts N2,000,000 in customer-induced debit transactions in a month, and the bank applies the maximum permissible Current Account Maintenance Fee rate. Approximately how much would this generate in CAMF, at the ceiling rate of N1 per mille?
opts: About N200 in fees
About N2,000 in fees
About N20,000 in fees
About N200,000 in fees
questionBank.exp: N1 per mille means N1 per N1,000. On N2,000,000 in customer-induced debit transactions, that works out to 2,000,000 ÷ 1,000 = N2,000 at the ceiling rate. N200 undercounts by a factor of ten, while N20,000 and N200,000 both overstate the mille calculation by one or two orders of magnitude.

questionBank.q: A customer transfers N500,000 from their current account to their own savings account at a different branch of the same bank. Should CAMF apply to this debit?
opts: Yes, since it is a customer-induced debit transaction
No — transfers between accounts in the same name are exempt
Yes, but only at half the standard CAMF rate
No, but only if the transfer is below N1,000,000
questionBank.exp: CAMF explicitly does not apply to debits representing a transfer to other accounts in the same name, whether at the same branch or another branch of the same bank — this transaction fits that exemption regardless of amount. Treating it as a standard chargeable debit, applying a discounted half-rate, or making the exemption conditional on a value threshold all misstate the rule.

questionBank.q: A customer sends an electronic transfer of N8,500 to a third party. Should the N50 Electronic Fund Transfer Levy apply?
opts: Yes, since all electronic transfers attract the levy regardless of amount
No — the levy only applies to transfers over N10,000
Yes, but only half the levy applies below N10,000
No, because the levy applies only to international transfers
questionBank.exp: The EFT Levy of N50 applies specifically to electronic transfers of amounts over N10,000; a N8,500 transfer falls below that threshold and is not levied. There's no general rule taxing all transfers regardless of size, no half-levy tier, and the levy is not restricted to international transfers — it applies to qualifying domestic transfers too.

questionBank.q: A customer withdraws N50,000 from their own savings account at an ATM. Does this transaction attract the Electronic Fund Transfer Levy?
opts: Yes, since the amount exceeds the N10,000 threshold
No — Savings Account withdrawals are exempt from the levy
Yes, but the levy is capped at N25 for savings accounts
No, but only for withdrawals made outside banking hours
questionBank.exp: Withdrawals or transfers from a Savings Account are specifically exempted from the EFT Levy, regardless of the amount involved. There's no capped reduced levy for savings accounts, and the exemption isn't conditioned on the time of the transaction — the account type itself is what triggers the exemption.

questionBank.q: What was a stated objective of the CBN and Bankers' Committee in launching the Bank Verification Number (BVN)?
opts: To replace the need for account opening documentation entirely
To identify and verify each customer across all banks
To set the interest rate payable on savings accounts industry-wide
To determine which products a customer is eligible to purchase
questionBank.exp: A stated BVN objective is providing a single means of identifying and verifying each customer's identity across all banks in Nigeria, curbing identity theft and strengthening service delivery. It doesn't replace account-opening documentation, set industry interest rates, or determine product eligibility — those are separate regulatory and commercial functions.

questionBank.q: A customer phones the bank to place a stop payment order on a cheque. What must happen next, per the bank's procedure for telephone-based stop payment instructions?
opts: The instruction is rejected until the customer visits the branch in person
The instruction is accepted but must be backed up with written confirmation within a specified time
The instruction is escalated to the CBN for verification before action
The instruction is only valid if given by the account's original signatory in writing beforehand
questionBank.exp: Stop payment instructions may be accepted by telephone, but must be backed up with written confirmation within a specified time, in line with SOP. Outright rejection pending an in-person visit, CBN escalation, or requiring prior written authorization all overstate the barrier — telephone instructions are valid on their own, subject to timely written follow-up.

questionBank.q: A customer's complaint about a wrongly debited transaction is investigated and found valid. Beyond correcting the error, what does the handling process require regarding the customer's position?
opts: The customer must accept a service credit instead of a cash refund
The customer must be properly restituted and not made to suffer any loss
The customer must file a written waiver before restitution is processed
The customer must escalate the complaint to Internal Audit before restitution
questionBank.exp: Complaints handling requires that the customer be properly restituted and not made to suffer any loss in any form, once a complaint is validated. Forcing a service credit instead of a refund, demanding a waiver, or requiring escalation to Internal Audit before restitution all add barriers the process doesn't call for.

questionBank.q: In the Barikisu Yede case, a fraudulent customer in a separate location was able to view and transact on the company's account after onboarding. What was the underlying cause that enabled this exposure?
opts: The company failed to submit a Board Resolution authorizing account opening
The onboarding officer captured the wrong phone number and signature, giving another customer access
The Ipaja branch lacked a functioning cheque book fireproof cabinet
The company's account was opened without a Certificate of Incorporation
questionBank.exp: The case is explicit that Susan Eyo, the onboarding officer, captured the wrong phone number and signature for the signatory, which made the account's transactions accessible to another customer entirely. Missing Board Resolutions, cheque-book storage, or a missing incorporation certificate are not mentioned as factors — the breach traces to a data-capture error at onboarding, a Client Information Services failure rather than a Security Function or documentation lapse.

questionBank.q: In the same case, when the fraudulent customer called to report unusual account access, the bank asked him to put it in writing before acting — and more funds were withdrawn within 24 hours. What does this response illustrate about the complaints handling process?
opts: That written confirmation is always required before a bank may act on any report
That requiring formal writing before urgent action delayed correction and increased customer loss
That verbal reports of fraud should be redirected to the CBN rather than the bank
That the customer making the report should have been treated as a suspect rather than a reporter
questionBank.exp: Handling customer complaints calls for prompt investigation and immediate correction to prevent repeat or escalating loss — insisting on written confirmation before acting, in a live fraud scenario, delayed the bank's response and let further withdrawals occur. This isn't a case for a blanket writing requirement (A), redirecting reports to the CBN (C), or treating the caller as a suspect (D) — the guide framework calls for prompt investigation and correction, not procedural gatekeeping, when funds are actively at risk.

questionBank.q: Which unit, alongside the CSU, is described as the primary entry point through which customers form their first impression of a bank?
opts: Treasury Operations desk
The Cash & Teller Unit (CTU)
Internal Control unit
Foreign Operations desk
questionBank.exp: The CTU is described as the primary entry into a bank — the window through which customers judge staff attitude and officer efficiency. Treasury Operations processes money-market transactions rather than walk-in customers, Internal Control checks SOP compliance, and Foreign Operations handles import/export transactions — none serve as the customer's first point of contact.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the acceptable features a CTU should maintain?
opts: Teller Tills may be freely shared between staff to save space
Customers should not wait endlessly, and documents should be time-stamped
Cash Holding Limits are set individually by each teller
Vault Operations are optional depending on branch size
questionBank.exp: Acceptable CTU features specifically include customers not waiting endlessly and time-stamping of all documents received. Teller Tills should never be shared (the opposite of A), cash holding limits are set by policy rather than by individual tellers, and Vault Operations are a required feature, not optional — so B is the only accurate statement among the four.

questionBank.q: A branch supervisor is not physically present in the banking hall at a given moment. Which CTU feature helps maintain area supervision despite this absence?
opts: The Teller Cash Holding Limit
CCTV
The Vault-In Register
The Teller Proof sheet
questionBank.exp: CCTV is specifically noted as useful for teller area supervision especially when the supervisor is not directly in the banking hall, alongside fraud monitoring and deterrence. The Teller Cash Holding Limit caps how much cash a teller may hold, the Vault-In Register tracks vault movement, and the Teller Proof sheet summarizes daily activity — none provide real-time visual oversight of the hall.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a basic skill a Teller should have, distinct from their personal qualities?
opts: Courage
Numeric skills
Honesty and Integrity
Enthusiasm
questionBank.exp: Numeric skills are listed under Basic Skills of a Teller, alongside communication, interpersonal, listening, problem-solving, and discerning skills. Courage, honesty and integrity, and enthusiasm are listed separately under Teller Qualities — a related but distinct category from skills.

questionBank.q: A teller answers a customer's phone call and chats casually with a colleague while other customers are waiting to be served. Which listed "Teller Don't" does this violate?
opts: Eating in the cubicle in front of a waiting customer
Using a mobile phone or chatting with a colleague while customers wait
Frowning at customers
Shouting at customers
questionBank.exp: Using mobile phones while attending to customers and chatting with another teller while customers are waiting are both explicitly listed Teller Don'ts, matching this scenario exactly. Eating, frowning, and shouting are separate listed don'ts describing different unprofessional behaviors, not the one illustrated here.

questionBank.q: A customer approaches a teller to purchase Business Travel Allowance ahead of an upcoming trip. Under the CTU's listed functions, which category does this fall under?
opts: Departmental Proof Duties
Basic foreign monies transactions
Government collections
Cash pick-ups and cash in transit
questionBank.exp: Business Travel Allowance (BTA) is explicitly listed as one of the Basic foreign monies transactions handled by the CTU, alongside Personal Travel Allowance, Domiciliary, and External Accounts. Departmental Proof Duties concerns end-of-day reconciliation, Government collections concerns items like Customs duties or FGN/State taxes, and cash pick-ups concern physical cash logistics between locations — none match a BTA purchase.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a CTU function alongside handling deposits and withdrawals?
opts: Setting the bank's overall interest rate policy
Fraud prevention / whistle blowing
Approving corporate loan facilities
Auditing the bank's annual financial statements
questionBank.exp: Fraud prevention / whistle blowing is listed as a distinct CTU function, alongside cheque processing, cash movements, and statutory compliance such as cashless policy. Setting interest rate policy, approving loans, and annual financial statement audits are functions of other units entirely — Treasury, Credit, and Internal Audit respectively — not the CTU.

questionBank.q: A customer walks in to make a cash deposit into their savings account. Under the CTU's listed customer-facing purposes, is this activity covered?
opts: No, deposits are handled exclusively by the CSU
Yes, a listed reason customers visit the CTU
No, only transfers are handled at the CTU
Yes, but only for corporate accounts
questionBank.exp: Depositing cash or cheque into an account is explicitly listed as one of the reasons customers go to the CTU, alongside withdrawals and transfers. It's not exclusive to the CSU, it's not limited to transfers only, and it's not restricted to corporate accounts — the listed purpose covers ordinary savings deposits like this one directly.

questionBank.q: Beyond processing transactions, tellers are expected to inform customers about new loans, credit cards, or investment options. Which teller responsibility does this describe?
opts: Account inquiries
Product and service promotion
Cheque transactions
Cash transactions
questionBank.exp: Product and service promotion is the responsibility covering informing customers about new products, services, and promotions such as loans, credit cards, or investment options. Account inquiries concerns balance and transaction questions, cheque transactions concerns processing and clearance information, and cash transactions concerns handling deposits and withdrawals — none involve proactively promoting other bank offerings.

questionBank.q: A teller is well-groomed, greets customers warmly, and handles a busy queue without visible frustration. Which listed Teller Quality is most directly demonstrated by remaining composed under a heavy queue?
opts: Neat and welcoming
Courageous
Enthusiasm
Speed and accuracy
questionBank.exp: Courageous is listed as a Teller Quality, reflecting the composure needed to handle pressure-filled situations such as a demanding queue without losing professionalism. Neat and welcoming concerns appearance and greeting, Enthusiasm concerns energy and attitude, and Speed and accuracy concerns transaction execution — while all are relevant qualities, staying composed under sustained pressure most directly reflects courage rather than these others.

questionBank.q: With the growth of ATMs and online banking, what role do bank tellers continue to play?
opts: They are being phased out entirely in favor of self-service channels
They continue providing personalized assistance and handling complex transactions requiring human interaction
They now handle only foreign currency transactions
They are reassigned exclusively to back-office reconciliation duties
questionBank.exp: Despite the rise of self-service channels, tellers continue to play a vital role in personalized assistance and conducting more complex transactions that require human interaction. They are not being phased out, not restricted to only FCY transactions, and not reassigned exclusively to back-office work — human tellers remain central to complex, judgment-requiring interactions.

questionBank.q: A teller arrives at work and finds cash left in their cubicle from the previous day, with no record of whose it is. What is the required treatment of this cash?
opts: Keep it in the till box until the owner is identified
Treat it as "Cash Found on Premises" with GL booking
Add it to the day's opening cash balance without further action
Report it to the CBN as unclaimed funds
questionBank.exp: Cash found in a teller cubicle or cash area must be investigated and treated as "Cash Found on Premises," handed to the Cash Officer, and booked in the GL with approval. Holding it informally, silently folding it into opening balance, or reporting straight to the CBN all bypass the required internal investigation and booking procedure.

questionBank.q: At the beginning of the day, who is responsible for opening the vault using dual keys and a combination?
opts: Any teller who arrives first
The Vault Custodian and Operation Head, as designated in writing
The branch's Head of Cash acting alone
The Customer Service Unit supervisor
questionBank.exp: The Vault Custodian and Operation Head, as designated in writing, open the vault with dual keys and combination at the start of the day — a dual-control arrangement, not a single individual's task. Any teller arriving first, the Head of Cash acting alone, or a CSU supervisor are not authorized to perform this dual-control opening.

questionBank.q: During the day, a teller finds their cash drawer has gone beyond the cubicle limit. What must the teller do?
opts: Continue transacting and adjust the limit at end of day
Evacuate the excess cash into the vault
Transfer the excess to a colleague's till without documentation
Hold the excess until the next business day
questionBank.exp: During the day, if a teller's cash goes beyond the cubicle limit, they need to evacuate cash into the vault, completing a teller transfer slip for the movement. Continuing to transact over the limit, transferring cash informally without documentation, or holding excess cash overnight all bypass the required evacuation and documentation procedure.

questionBank.q: At the end of the day, a teller finds a cash difference between the system balance and physical cash on hand. What is the first required step?
opts: Post the difference directly into the Cash Difference Account
Print the transaction journal and do a call over
Report the matter immediately to the CBN
Close the till box and investigate the next morning
questionBank.exp: Where a cash difference is found, the teller must print the transaction journal and do a call over as the first step; only if the difference persists is it escalated to a supervisor, and posting to the Cash Difference Account requires supervisor approval after that. Reporting straight to the CBN or deferring investigation to the next day both skip the immediate call-over step the procedure requires.

questionBank.q: At the end of the day, a teller's cash balances exactly with the system, with no discrepancy at all. What does the procedure still require the teller to do?
opts: Nothing further, since a balanced position needs no additional documentation
Print the transaction journal and do a call over to detect qualitative errors
Skip the proof sheet, since it is only required when a difference exists
Report directly to Internal Control before closing
questionBank.exp: Even with no cash difference, the teller must still print the transaction journal and do a call over, to detect qualitative errors such as posting into the wrong customer account — a balanced cash position doesn't guarantee error-free postings. Skipping documentation, omitting the proof sheet, or reporting to Internal Control instead of following the standard proof procedure would all leave posting errors undetected.

questionBank.q: At the very end of the vault-locking process, who locks the vault using dual control keys and combination?
opts: The teller with the highest cash balance for the day
The Vault Custodian and Head of Operation
The Customer Service Unit supervisor on duty
Any two tellers designated at random
questionBank.exp: The Vault Custodian and Head of Operation lock the vault using the dual control keys and combination number, mirroring the same dual-control pairing used to open it in the morning. A teller acting alone by cash volume, a CSU supervisor, or randomly designated tellers are not the parties authorized for this final dual-control step.

questionBank.q: While processing a cash deposit, a teller notices the cash counted is short of the amount written on the deposit slip. What must the teller do at this point in the procedure?
opts: Adjust the deposit slip to match the counted cash without informing the customer
Notify the customer of the discrepancy encountered
Reject the deposit outright and end the transaction
Credit the account for the higher amount and resolve later
questionBank.exp: The procedure requires the teller to notify the customer of any discrepancy, whether shortage or overage, encountered during counting. Silently adjusting the slip, rejecting the deposit outright, or crediting the higher unverified amount all bypass this required customer notification step.

questionBank.q: Under the standard cash deposit procedure, who is prohibited from preparing or altering a customer's deposit slip?
opts: The customer themselves
The Teller or Note Counter
The Cash Officer
The Head of Operations
questionBank.exp: The procedure explicitly states that under no circumstance should a Teller or Note Counter prepare or alter a Deposit Slip for a customer — this is a customer-completed document. The customer is meant to complete it themselves, while the Cash Officer and Head of Operations are not mentioned as parties who prepare deposit slips at all, so the restriction specifically targets the Teller/Note Counter role.

questionBank.q: A customer submits a US$1,000 foreign currency withdrawal ticket. Given a 1% commission and 7.5% VAT charged on that commission, how much total is debited from the customer beyond the US$1,000 principal?
questionBank.exp: 1% commission on US$1,000 is US$10. VAT of 7.5% is then charged on the commission, not the principal: 7.5% of US$10 = US$0.75. Total additional debit = US$10 + US$0.75 = US$10.75. US$7.50 misapplies the VAT rate to the principal instead of the commission, US$17.50 wrongly adds a flat 7.5% of principal on top of commission-based VAT, and US$75.00 mistakes the VAT base entirely.

questionBank.q: For a foreign currency cash withdrawal, which entry correctly credits the customer's withdrawn US Dollar cash, per the illustrated FCY withdrawal entries?
opts: Debit the US$ Cash Account, reversing the correct direction
Credit US$ Cash Account, using code and customer name
Credit the Commission Account for the Naira equivalent
Debit the customer's account for the withdrawal value
questionBank.exp: The FCY withdrawal entries specifically Credit the US$ Cash Account using the appropriate code and the customer's name as text — the bank's cash account is credited as cash physically leaves. Debiting the US$ Cash Account reverses the correct direction, crediting the Commission Account is a separate entry for the fee income, and debiting the customer's account is also correct but describes a different leg of the same transaction, not the one asked about here.

questionBank.q: A customer deposits cash after the branch's System Cut Off Time. What happens to the credit entry to the customer's account under the Late Cash Deposit procedure?
opts: The credit is passed immediately, backdated to the current day
The credit is deferred to the following business day
The deposit is rejected until the next morning
The credit is passed at half value pending verification
questionBank.exp: Under Late Cash Deposit procedure, cash is verified and counted in the customer's presence, but entries are not passed to the customer's account until the following business day, due to the end-of-day system run. Immediate backdated crediting, outright rejection of the deposit, or a half-value interim credit are not features of this procedure — the cash is still accepted and recorded, just credited a day later.

questionBank.q: A corporate customer has a binding legal agreement with the bank for cash picked up from their premises, processed under "Subject to Count." What happens to the customer's account entries under this arrangement?
opts: Entries are passed only after the cash is fully detail-counted
Entries are passed immediately, with detailed counting completed within 24 hours
Entries are passed after a 7-day verification hold
Entries are never passed until a dispute-free reconciliation is confirmed
questionBank.exp: Under Subject to Count (STC) processing, entries are passed immediately (Debit Cash, Credit customer's account), with the detailed count of cash completed within 24 hours as per SOP — the legal agreement in place allows this immediate crediting ahead of full verification. Waiting for full counting first, a 7-day hold, or an indefinite dispute-free requirement all contradict the defining feature of STC, which is immediate crediting.

questionBank.q: A drawer and payee both hold accounts at the same bank, and the payee deposits the drawer's cheque into their account. Under the In-House Account-to-Account Transfer procedure, what must the payee do on the back of the cheque?
opts: Nothing — only the drawer's signature is required
Write their name, phone number, and sign
Attach a copy of their means of identification
Obtain a countersignature from the branch manager
questionBank.exp: The procedure requires the Payee to write name, phone number, and sign on the back of the cheque, as part of the in-house transfer process. The drawer's signature is verified separately against their mandate, an attached ID copy is a third-party payee requirement rather than an in-house transfer step, and a branch manager countersignature is not part of this procedure.

questionBank.q: A cheque drawn on another bank, payable to the branch's own customer, is deposited. Per the Bankers' Clearing House Rules referenced in the procedure, when does this Other Bank's Cheque (OBC) typically reflect value?
opts: Same day, immediately upon deposit
Forward value date, T+1
After a mandatory 5 business day hold
Only after the drawee bank confirms funds by phone
questionBank.exp: OBC deposits are processed with a forward value date, T+1, in line with the Bankers' Clearing House Rules. Same-day value doesn't apply since it must clear through another bank first, a flat 5-day hold overstates the timeline referenced, and phone-based confirmation from the drawee bank is not the mechanism described for standard OBC value dating.

questionBank.q: An OBC cheque made payable to a corporate body is presented for credit to a personal account. What must the teller do with this cheque?
opts: Process it normally, since payee type doesn't restrict OBC cheques
Refer it to the Cash Officer, since this is a conversion
Reject it outright with no further review possible
Credit it automatically once MICR is confirmed
questionBank.exp: Cheques payable to a corporate body and endorsed for credit to a personal account are specifically flagged as a conversion, requiring referral to the Cash Officer or Head of Cash for review. Processing it as routine ignores this named risk category, outright rejection with no review skips the referral step that's actually required, and MICR encoding confirmation alone doesn't address the conversion concern.

questionBank.q: A teller's cash on hand at balancing is less than the system and Teller Proof figures suggest. Which of the following is listed as a possible cause of this specific situation?
opts: Deliberate under-payment to a customer
Overpayment to a customer
Cash lodgment exceeding the amount on the deposit slip
Mixing personal money with the bank's funds
questionBank.exp: Overpayment to customers is listed as a cause of Cash Shortage — physical cash lower than system and proof figures. Deliberate under-payment, cash lodgment exceeding the deposit slip amount, and mixing personal money with bank funds are all listed instead as causes of Cash Overage (surplus), the opposite situation, since each would leave the teller holding more cash than the records show.

questionBank.q: A teller's cash on hand at balancing is more than the system and Teller Proof figures suggest. Which of the following is listed as a possible cause of this specific situation?
opts: Pilfering by the teller from their own till
A customer being short paid
Total amount on the deposit slip exceeding the physical cash received
Error in the posting of a transaction
questionBank.exp: A customer being short paid is listed as a cause of Cash Overage — physical cash higher than system and proof figures, since the bank retained cash it should have paid out. Pilfering, a deposit-slip total exceeding physical cash received, and general posting errors are listed instead as causes of Cash Shortage, the opposite situation.

questionBank.q: After identifying a cash difference and it cannot be resolved through a call over, what is the required escalation sequence before posting to the Cash Difference Account?
opts: Post to the Cash Difference Account immediately without escalation
Escalate to a supervisor, redo the call over, then post with approval
Escalate directly to the CBN for a ruling
Wait until month-end to post all accumulated differences at once
questionBank.exp: If a difference persists, it's reported to the supervisor, who assigns another teller to redo the call over; only if still unresolved is approval sought to post the difference into the Cash Difference Account. Posting immediately without escalation skips the required verification step, CBN escalation is not part of this internal procedure, and waiting until month-end contradicts the same-day resolution process described.

questionBank.q: A staff member presents an Internal Payment Order / Cash Ticket for payment. Before validating and paying cash, what must the teller check on the ticket?
opts: Only the beneficiary's employee ID number
Authentication/approval from appropriate authorities, and the beneficiary's signature on the back
A prior three-month transaction history for the beneficiary
Confirmation from the CSU that the beneficiary has an active account
questionBank.exp: The procedure requires checking for authentication/approval from appropriate authorities and having the beneficiary write their name and sign on the back of the ticket, before validating and paying. An employee ID check alone, a transaction-history pull, or CSU account confirmation are not the checks this internal-ticket procedure specifies.

questionBank.q: A cheque presented for withdrawal shows an amount exceeding the customer's account balance. What is required before this withdrawal can be processed?
opts: The withdrawal is processed automatically, taking the account into overdraft
Additional approvals are required for withdrawals on unfunded accounts
The teller pays out from petty cash instead of the customer account
The cheque is forwarded to Treasury Operations for funding
questionBank.exp: Withdrawals on unfunded accounts and accounts with incomplete documentation require additional approvals — this is a control point, not an automatic pass-through. Automatic overdraft processing, paying from petty cash, or forwarding to Treasury are not part of the standard withdrawal procedure for an unfunded account.

questionBank.q: A customer requests a withdrawal from a savings account that would take the balance below zero. What does the procedure say about this?
opts: It is permitted with supervisor approval only
A savings account cannot be thrown into debit
It is permitted up to a fixed overdraft limit
It is permitted if the customer signs an indemnity
questionBank.exp: The procedure states plainly that a savings account cannot be thrown into debit — this is a hard rule, not a matter requiring approval, a limit, or an indemnity. None of the other options are recognized workarounds; a savings account withdrawal exceeding the available balance simply cannot be processed.

questionBank.q: A third party, not the account holder, presents a cheque for payment over the counter. What must the teller obtain from this third-party payee before payment?
opts: A letter of introduction from the account holder's employer
Acceptable means of identification, e.g. International Passport, National ID, or Driver's License
A notarized affidavit of identity
A guarantee from another existing customer of the bank
questionBank.exp: For third-party payees, the procedure requires obtaining acceptable means of identification such as an International Passport, National ID, Driver's License, or acceptable company ID, in line with policy. An employer letter, a notarized affidavit, or a guarantor customer are not the identification routes this procedure specifies.

questionBank.q: Under Vault Operations, who holds overall dual control of the vault, per the arrangement described?
opts: Any two tellers on duty that day
The Vault Custodian and the Branch Services Manager
The Head Teller and the CSU supervisor
The Cash Officer acting alone with a master key
questionBank.exp: The vault must be under Dual Control, which may be the Vault Custodian and the Branch Services Manager, per the described arrangement. Any two tellers, a Head Teller/CSU pairing, or a single Cash Officer with a master key do not match this specific dual-control structure.

questionBank.q: Which of the following personnel is described as supervising the Tellers directly, distinct from supervising the wider Operations function?
opts: Branch Services Manager
Head Teller
Head of Operations
Vault Custodian
questionBank.exp: The Head Teller is listed as the role that supervises the Tellers specifically. The Head of Operations supervises Operations more broadly, the Branch Services Manager is in charge of Branch Services, and the Vault Custodian is in charge of the Vault itself — each a distinct role from direct teller supervision.

questionBank.q: What is the purpose of the Teller Cash Exchange/Transfer Ticket, as described under Vault Operations?
opts: To record customer complaints about cash shortages
To document any cash movement between tellers and head tellers
To authorize a teller's annual leave request
To record CCTV footage retention schedules
questionBank.exp: Tellers must fill a cash exchange ticket for any cash movement between tellers and head tellers — it exists specifically to document cash changing hands internally. Complaint recording, leave authorization, and CCTV retention are unrelated administrative matters this ticket does not cover.

questionBank.q: A company with multiple divisions and collection points arranges for the bank to regularly collect cash from each location under a standing agreement. Which listed source of cash deposits into the vault does this describe?
opts: Local Collection
Cash Sweep
Proceeds from Disposal of Bank Assets
Withdrawals from CBN
questionBank.exp: Cash Sweep is the service described for a company with many divisions or outlets and multiple collection points, usually under a Standing Instruction agreement. Local Collection is a similar but more irregular, fee-based service without the multi-division standing arrangement, while Disposal of Bank Assets and CBN withdrawals are unrelated internal/regulatory cash sources.

questionBank.q: What does the Teller's Departmental Proof Sheet primarily show, as prepared at the end of each day?
opts: The teller's annual leave balance record
A daily summary of till balance and cash by denomination
The branch's total loan portfolio value
Complaint timelines
questionBank.exp: The Proof Sheet shows the summary of activities at the Teller point in a day, including till balance and cash by denomination, closing cash totals, and any difference. Leave balances, loan portfolios, and complaint timelines are unrelated to this daily cash-focused reconciliation document.

questionBank.q: After receiving all tellers' proof sheets, what must the Head Teller/Cash Officer do regarding interdepartmental postings?
opts: Ignore them, since they fall outside the departmental proof process
Verify interdepartmental postings to agree differences, if any, and make necessary postings
Forward them unreviewed directly to the CBN
Delete any postings that do not immediately reconcile
questionBank.exp: The Head Teller/Cash Officer must verify interdepartmental postings to agree any differences and make the necessary postings, as part of combining all tellers' proofs. Ignoring interdepartmental items, forwarding unreviewed data to the CBN, or deleting unreconciled postings all bypass the required verification step.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a Key Control for tellers to observe in daily cash operations?
opts: Share passwords only with the branch manager
Balance cash every 2 to 3 hours
Review the SOP only at year-end
Escalate irregularities only after month-end close
questionBank.exp: Balancing cash every 2 to 3 hours is listed as a Key Control, alongside protecting passwords and escalating irregularities promptly. Sharing passwords with anyone (even a manager) contradicts the "do not share passwords" control, reviewing the SOP only at year-end understates how often it should be reviewed, and escalating irregularities only after month-end contradicts the requirement to escalate promptly.

questionBank.q: What is one purpose control measures in cash operations are meant to serve, alongside completeness and integrity of information?
opts: Maximizing the branch's daily transaction volume
Protection against possible liability from negligence, conversion, defamation, or fraud
Reducing the number of tellers required per shift
Increasing the branch's cash holding limit
questionBank.exp: Control measures are meant to protect against possible liability from negligence, conversion, defamation, and fraud, alongside ensuring completeness and integrity of information. Maximizing transaction volume, reducing staffing, and increasing cash holding limits are operational or capacity goals, not the stated purpose of these controls.

questionBank.q: Sarah, the bank teller in the closing case study, resumes well before the bank opens to customers. Which daily-flow principle does this most directly reflect?
opts: The requirement to balance cash every 2–3 hours
Resuming earlier than 7:30am, ready before customers arrive
Completing a Teller Cash Exchange Ticket
Reconciling interdepartmental postings
questionBank.exp: The Beginning of Day procedure specifically requires resuming earlier than 7:30am and being ready for work before the bank opens — Sarah's early arrival mirrors this exactly. Balancing every 2–3 hours applies during the day rather than at arrival, the Cash Exchange Ticket concerns inter-teller movements, and interdepartmental reconciliation is an end-of-day Head Teller task, not a reflection of early resumption.

questionBank.q: Over the course of her day, Sarah handles deposits, withdrawals, and customer questions while maintaining accuracy and courtesy. Which combination of factors does the case study ask trainees to highlight in her role?
opts: Only her speed in processing transactions
Customer service, financial accuracy, and security/compliance standards, together
Only her compliance with CCTV monitoring
Only her ability to promote new products
questionBank.exp: The case study's prompt specifically asks for 5 key areas showing Sarah's role in customer service, financial accuracy, and security/compliance standards together — a rounded professional performance, not one isolated skill. Isolating only speed, only CCTV compliance, or only product promotion each captures a single slice rather than the multi-dimensional role the case study asks trainees to analyze.

questionBank.q: If Sarah discovers a cash shortage while balancing at the end of her day, what does the daily-flow procedure require her to do first?
opts: Post it immediately to the Cash Difference Account
Print the transaction journal and perform a call over
Inform the customer who made the last transaction of the day
Wait until the next morning to investigate
questionBank.exp: As with any teller balancing discrepancy, Sarah's first step is to print the transaction journal and do a call over; escalation to a supervisor and posting to the Cash Difference Account only follow if the difference isn't resolved. Posting immediately, informing an unrelated customer, or delaying investigation to the next day all skip this required first step.

questionBank.q: When Sarah handles a customer request that falls outside routine deposits and withdrawals, such as a query about cheque clearance timing, which of her core responsibilities is she drawing on?
opts: Cash transactions, handling physical currency
Cheque transactions, covering clearance and funds availability
Product and service promotion efforts
Vault Operations, a back-of-house function
questionBank.exp: Cheque transactions responsibilities specifically include providing information on cheque clearance and funds availability, matching this kind of customer query. Cash transactions concern handling physical currency, product promotion concerns informing customers about new offerings, and Vault Operations is a distinct back-of-house function Sarah, as a front-line teller, does not directly perform.

questionBank.q: At the close of her shift, Sarah returns her cash box to the vault alongside the Vault Custodian, and both sign the Vault Record Book. What is the purpose of this joint signing?
opts: To confirm Sarah's attendance for payroll purposes
To document dual accountability, matching the dual-control principle used throughout vault operations
To authorize Sarah's access to the vault the next morning
To record the CCTV footage timestamp for the day
questionBank.exp: The dual signing documents joint accountability for the returned cash box, consistent with the dual-control principle that governs vault access throughout the day (opening, movement, and closing all require paired sign-off). It is not a payroll attendance record, doesn't itself authorize next-day access (that requires the next morning's own dual-control opening), and is unrelated to CCTV timestamping.

questionBank.q: Considering the case study holistically, why does the manual frame "a day in the life of a Bank Teller" around Sarah specifically, rather than describing procedures in the abstract?
opts: Because procedures differ significantly for every individual teller
Because a lived day shows how service, accuracy, and compliance interact together
Because Sarah's case reveals a specific instance of teller misconduct to be avoided
Because the case study replaces the need to learn the formal Beginning/During/End of Day procedures
questionBank.exp: The case study's framing device is to walk through a single day so trainees see how customer service, financial accuracy, and security/compliance standards interact in a lived sequence, rather than as isolated abstract rules. Procedures don't differ per teller (A), the case does not depict misconduct (C) — Sarah is presented positively — and it supplements rather than replaces the formal Beginning/During/End of Day procedures covered earlier in the module (D).

questionBank.q: Which skill is specifically described as being measured directly at the Teller points, distinct from courtesy or speed of service?
opts: Product cross-selling ability
Queue management skill
Foreign language proficiency
Data entry accuracy
questionBank.exp: Queue management skill is specifically noted as measured at the Teller points, alongside speed of service and visible courtesy — all things a customer can observe directly in an open banking hall. Cross-selling ability, language proficiency, and data entry accuracy are not the skill highlighted as being measured at this specific customer-facing point.

questionBank.q: How is a Bank Teller most accurately described in terms of their position within a bank branch?
opts: A back-office risk officer, no customer contact
A front-line professional, often first point of contact
A regulatory examiner monitoring compliance
A relationship manager for corporate accounts
questionBank.exp: A bank teller is described as a banking professional who works at the front line of a branch and is often the first point of contact for customers visiting the bank. A back-office risk officer, a regulatory examiner, and a corporate relationship manager all describe different roles with different scopes than the front-line, customer-facing teller position.

questionBank.q: A customer asks a teller to confirm their recent transaction history and current balance. Which teller responsibility covers this request?
opts: Cheque transactions
Account inquiries
Cash transactions
Product and service promotion
questionBank.exp: Account inquiries specifically covers assisting customers with questions about account balances, recent transactions, and account-related matters. Cheque and cash transactions concern processing physical instruments and currency, while product promotion concerns informing customers about new offerings — none match a request for balance and transaction history.

questionBank.q: While processing a foreign currency cash deposit, the teller compares the name on the deposit slip with the name on the system. What is the purpose of this specific check?
opts: To determine the applicable exchange rate
To ensure correctness before the deposit is processed
To calculate the commission payable on the deposit
To verify the customer's Bank Verification Number
questionBank.exp: The FCY deposit procedure includes comparing the name on the slip with the name on the system specifically to ensure correctness — a basic identity-matching control before proceeding. It is not used to determine an exchange rate, calculate commission (deposits generally don't attract the withdrawal-style commission), or verify a BVN, which is a separate check entirely.

questionBank.q: A teller processing a cheque withdrawal notices the cheque's serial number falls outside the range the system expects for that customer. What does the system do in this situation?
opts: Process the withdrawal normally, since serial numbers are informational only
Flag the transaction as outside the customer's or bank's allowed range
Automatically reject the cheque with no override possible
Silently correct the serial number based on the account history
questionBank.exp: The system will flag where the cheque's serial number is outside the range issued to the customer or outside the range allowed by the bank — a control against cloned or unauthorized instruments. Processing it as routine ignores this flag, automatic rejection with no override overstates the response (an override request is possible under policy), and silently correcting the number is not a described system behavior.

questionBank.q: A teller wants to pay out an amount above their individually assigned Teller's Limit. What must happen before this payment can proceed?
opts: The teller may proceed once the customer signs an indemnity
A request for override above the Teller's Limit must be made
The payment is automatically declined with no recourse
The teller may split the payment into smaller transactions to stay under the limit
questionBank.exp: Amounts above a Teller's Limit require a request for override, referred as part of the endorsement/approval checks in the withdrawal procedure. A customer indemnity, an automatic decline with no recourse, or artificially splitting the payment to dodge the limit are not the sanctioned route — the procedure calls for a proper override request instead.
