questionBank.q: At the start of the day, each designated custodian unlocks the combination for their own side of the vault compartment. Who typically fills these two designated custodian roles?
opts: Two random tellers selected by the branch manager
Usually a Teller and the Cash Officer
The Head of Operations and the CSU supervisor
Any staff member holding a master key
questionBank.exp: Vault compartment operation is usually split between a Teller and the Cash Officer, each unlocking their own side of the compartment. Randomly selected tellers, a Head of Operations/CSU pairing, or generic master-key holders don't match the specific dual-role structure described for this step.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the sources of cash withdrawal from a branch, distinct from Savings, Current, and ATM withdrawals?
opts: Cash Sweep collections
Cash Advance / Payments for Operating Expenses
Foreign currency FCY tester verification
Vault-In Register entries
questionBank.exp: Cash Advance / Payments for Operating Expenses is listed among the Sources of Cash Withdrawal from a Branch, alongside Savings, Current, ATM, and other cash payment forms. Cash Sweep is a vault-deposit source rather than a withdrawal source, FCY tester verification is a genuineness check rather than a withdrawal type, and the Vault-In Register is a monitoring tool rather than a withdrawal category.

questionBank.q: Which combination of account types is listed under "Cash Deposit into Customers' Accounts" as a source of cash deposits into the vault?
opts: Only Corporate Current Accounts, per branch policy
Transaction, MMDA, savings, and small time deposit accounts
Only Domiciliary Accounts held offshore
Only accounts held by government agencies
questionBank.exp: The listed source covers transaction accounts, money market deposit accounts, savings accounts, and small time deposits — a broad mix of deposit account types feeding cash into the vault. Restricting this to only corporate current accounts, only Domiciliary accounts, or only government accounts each understates the actual breadth of accounts listed.

questionBank.q: After collecting all tellers' proofs, what is the final listed step the Head Teller/Cash Officer performs before matters move to Internal Controls?
opts: Destroy the proofs once totals match
Confirm and send proofs to Internal Controls after call-back
Forward the proofs directly to the CBN
File the proofs without verification
questionBank.exp: The final listed step has the Head Teller/Cash Officer confirming tickets and proofs and sending them to Internal Controls after call-back of transactions — a formal handover for independent review. Destroying the proofs, forwarding straight to the CBN, or filing them without verification all skip this required confirmation and handover step.

questionBank.q: Among the key personnel involved in Vault Operations, who is specifically described as being "in charge of the Vault" itself?
opts: Head of Operations
Vault Custodian
Branch Services Manager
Head Teller
questionBank.exp: The Vault Custodian is the role specifically described as being in charge of the Vault. The Head of Operations supervises Operations broadly, the Branch Services Manager is in charge of Branch Services generally, and the Head Teller supervises the Tellers — each a related but distinct role from direct vault custodianship.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as an acceptable CTU feature relating to how excess cash is managed over the course of the day?
opts: Excess cash should remain with the teller until end of day for convenience
Evacuation of excess cash from Tellers at regular intervals
Excess cash should be transferred directly to another branch daily
Excess cash should be converted to fixed deposits automatically
questionBank.exp: Evacuation of excess cash from Tellers at regular intervals is listed as an acceptable CTU feature, working alongside cash holding limits to keep teller cash exposure controlled throughout the day. Holding excess cash until end of day, transferring it to another branch daily, or auto-converting it to fixed deposits are not features described in this section.

questionBank.q: How can the layout and design of the Cash & Teller Area affect staff and customers, according to the module?
opts: It has no measurable effect on either group at all
It can be a source of motivation to staff and customers
It only affects customers, never affects staff
It determines the branch's cash holding limit
questionBank.exp: The layout and design of the CTU area is noted as a potential source of motivation to both staff and customers, alongside its role in first impressions. Claiming no effect, limiting the effect to customers only, or tying layout to cash holding limits (a separate policy matter) all misstate what the module says about layout and design.

questionBank.q: A third-party payee presents a cheque for an amount exceeding the maximum single amount payable over the counter under the cashless banking policy. What must the teller compare the cheque against before proceeding?
opts: Only the payee's identification document
The cashless banking maximum single amount, and other thresholds
The customer's historical average withdrawal amount
The branch's total cash holding limit for the day
questionBank.exp: The procedure requires comparing the cheque against the cashless banking requirement's maximum single amount payable over the counter to a third-party payee, and other regulatory thresholds. Checking identification alone, comparing to historical averages, or checking the branch's overall cash holding limit are separate matters that don't substitute for this specific cashless-policy comparison.

questionBank.q: What does the note about "zero balance in till boxes" at the end of day refer to, as practiced in some banks?
opts: A requirement that tellers hold no personal funds anywhere in the branch
A practice where tellers hold zero cash in their till box after evacuation
A rule that new tellers must start with a zero cash allocation on their first day
A requirement that the vault itself holds zero cash overnight, which would defeat its purpose
questionBank.exp: The note specifies that in some banks, tellers are required to have zero balance in their till boxes — meaning all cash is evacuated to the vault at end of day, leaving nothing in the till box itself overnight. It doesn't concern personal funds elsewhere in the branch, a new teller's starting allocation, or the vault holding zero cash (the vault is where the cash goes, not where it's absent).

questionBank.q: Among the Key Controls listed for cash operations, which one specifically relates to identifying potentially fraudulent behavior through account monitoring?
opts: Lock all PCs, drawers, and teller boxes when leaving your work area
Watch out for unusual patterns of transaction on customer accounts
Ensure all registers are completed and reviewed daily by supervisors
Review the SOP on all processes
questionBank.exp: Watching out for unusual patterns of transaction on customer accounts is the Key Control specifically aimed at spotting potential fraud through behavioral monitoring. Locking workstations, register review, and SOP review are all valuable controls too, but they concern physical/procedural discipline rather than pattern-based fraud detection on customer accounts.

questionBank.q: Which statutory provision established the Nigerian Bankers' Clearing House (NBCH)?
opts: S.47 of the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act
S.47 of the CBN Act No. 7 of 2007
S.61 of the Companies and Allied Matters Act
S.12 of the NIBSS Establishment Act
questionBank.exp: S.47 of the CBN Act No. 7 of 2007 is the specific provision that set up the NBCH. BOFIA, CAMA, and a NIBSS Establishment Act are real or plausible-sounding statutes governing other areas of banking, but none of them is the provision that created the NBCH itself.

questionBank.q: Which body currently plays the operational role the CBN used to play in Bankers' Clearing?
opts: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC)
Nigeria Interbank Settlement Systems (NIBSS)
The Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)
The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
questionBank.exp: NIBSS is now playing the role the CBN used to perform in Bankers' Clearing operations. NDIC insures deposits, CAC handles company registration, and SEC regulates capital markets — none of these bodies took over the CBN's operational clearing role.

questionBank.q: A non-member bank wants to have its cheques cleared through the NBCH system without becoming a full member itself. What route is available to it?
opts: It cannot clear cheques through the NBCH under any arrangement
It may enter an Agency Agreement with a Member of the NBCH
It must first obtain a special CBN clearing license unrelated to NBCH
It may clear directly through NIBSS bypassing all member banks
questionBank.exp: Non-member banks may enter into an Agency Agreement with any Member(s) of the NBCH, for clearing and collecting cheques on their behalf. Being locked out entirely, needing a separate special license, or bypassing member banks via NIBSS directly are not the described route — the agency arrangement is the actual mechanism.

questionBank.q: Who chairs the NBCH's management committee and appoints the Superintendent who presides over each clearing session?
opts: The Bankers' Committee, by majority vote
The CBN
NIBSS, as the operating body
The member bank with the largest settlement volume
questionBank.exp: The CBN appoints the Chairman, Superintendent, and Assistants, with the Superintendent acting as the boss at each clearing session. This appointment role is not held by the Bankers' Committee, by NIBSS as an operator, or by whichever bank happens to clear the largest volume.

questionBank.q: A bank persistently overdraws its Settlement Account maintained with the CBN. What consequence does this expose the bank to under NBCH rules?
opts: A formal warning letter with no further consequence
Suspension of the bank's NBCH membership
An automatic downgrade to non-settlement bank status only
A one-time fine with continued membership unaffected
questionBank.exp: Persistently overdrawing its Settlement Account is explicitly listed as a basis for suspension of an NBCH member. A mere warning letter, an automatic downgrade with no suspension, or a one-time fine with unaffected membership all understate the actual consequence — suspension is the rule's stated response.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is classified as a Paper Instrument eligible for clearing, rather than an Electronic Instrument?
opts: NIBSS Electronic Funds Transfer (NEFT)
Dividend Warrants
Automated Clearing House (ACH) transfers
Any instrument approved solely by NIBSS
questionBank.exp: Dividend Warrants are listed under Paper Instruments, alongside cheques, drafts, interest warrants, debit and credit notes, and bankers' payments. NEFT and ACH transfers are listed under Electronic Instruments instead, and eligible instruments must be approved by CBN, not solely by NIBSS.

questionBank.q: What governs the maximum amount an eligible financial instrument may carry when presented for clearing?
opts: Each bank sets its own internal maximum independently
A maximum amount approved by CBN
The maximum is fixed permanently at N10 million with no review
There is no maximum; any amount may be presented
questionBank.exp: Each eligible financial instrument presented for clearing shall not exceed the maximum amount as approved by CBN — a centrally set ceiling, not a bank-by-bank or unlimited arrangement. Independent bank-set maximums, a permanently fixed N10 million figure with no review, and an unlimited-amount claim all misstate this centrally governed ceiling.

questionBank.q: A Settlement Bank and a Non-Settlement Bank both need to maintain clearing collateral. Roughly how does the required collateral compare between the two?
opts: Both must maintain exactly the same amount of collateral
A Settlement Bank's collateral (N15 billion) is far larger than a Non-Settlement Bank's (N250 million)
A Non-Settlement Bank's collateral exceeds a Settlement Bank's
Only Settlement Banks are required to maintain any collateral at all
questionBank.exp: Settlement Banks maintain N15 billion in Clearing Collateral, while Non-Settlement Banks maintain N250 million — a roughly 60-fold difference reflecting their differing settlement responsibilities. Equal amounts, a reversed comparison, or exempting Non-Settlement Banks entirely all misstate the actual figures and the rule that both categories must maintain collateral.

questionBank.q: After each clearing session, what happens to a bank's Net Settlement Balance?
opts: It is carried forward indefinitely without being applied to any account
It is applied to the account the bank maintains with CBN
It is applied only to the bank's collateral holding, not its account balance
It is reported to NIBSS but not actually settled until month-end
questionBank.exp: The Net Settlement Balance of a bank is applied to the account maintained with CBN after each session — Settlement Banks to their Settlement Account, Non-Settlement Banks to their Operations Account. Carrying it forward indefinitely, applying it only to collateral, or deferring settlement to month-end all contradict the per-session application the rule describes.

questionBank.q: When did the new Nigeria Cheque Standard become fully operational, ending the parallel run of old and new cheques?
opts: September 2019
April 1, 2021
August 2007
March 31, 2015
questionBank.exp: The new Nigeria Cheque Standard became fully operational on April 1, 2021, though the parallel run of old and new cheques had started since September 2019. September 2019 marks the start of the parallel run rather than full operation, while August 2007 and March 31, 2015 relate to unconnected initiatives (PSV2020 launch and a CBN circular on dud cheques, respectively).

questionBank.q: A Paying Bank is unable to return a cheque within the clearing deadline. What is the deadline for it to serve a Special Caution Notice on the Presenting Bank?
opts: Immediately, with no grace period allowed
Two hours after the closure of the return cheque session
24 hours after the closure of the return cheque session
By the start of the next clearing session, whenever that falls
questionBank.exp: The deadline for submission of a Special Caution Notice is two hours after the closure of the return cheque session, per Clearing Rules 12.1.8. An immediate no-grace-period requirement, a 24-hour window, or an open-ended "next session" deadline all overstate or understate this specific two-hour window.

questionBank.q: A Special Caution Notice is served, but the Paying Bank fails to send the required debit note to the Presenting Bank within 2 working days. What happens as a result?
opts: The cheque is automatically dishonoured regardless of the delay
The Presenting Bank may give value without further recourse to the Paying Bank
The CBN automatically reverses the transaction
The Special Caution Notice becomes void and must be reissued
questionBank.exp: Where the Paying Bank fails to send a debit note within 2 working days, the Presenting Bank may give value without further recourse to the Paying Bank, per Clearing Rules 12.1.10. Automatic dishonour regardless of delay, CBN-initiated automatic reversal, and voiding the notice for reissue are not the rule's actual consequence — the failure shifts the practical outcome toward the Presenting Bank's favor instead.

questionBank.q: A Presenting Bank fails to honour a duly served Special Caution Notice, and the customer suffers a loss as a result. Who bears liability for this loss?
opts: The Paying Bank, since it issued the notice
The Presenting Bank, per section 12.1.9 of the Clearing Rules
The CBN, as regulator of the clearing system
The liability is shared equally between all clearing member banks
questionBank.exp: The Presenting Bank is fully liable where it fails to honour a Special Caution Notice, in line with section 12.1.9 of the Clearing Rules. The Paying Bank did its part by issuing the notice, the CBN is the regulator rather than a liable party in this specific failure, and liability is not spread across all member banks — it rests squarely on the Presenting Bank that ignored the notice.

questionBank.q: A cheque is returned because the account name on the cheque doesn't match the account number provided. Under the approved reasons for returning cheques, how would this be recorded on the instrument?
opts: Incomplete or Irregular Mandate
Account Name and Account number differ
Endorsement irregular
Blurred or Blank Image
questionBank.exp: "Account Name and Account number differ" is a specific approved reason listed for returning a cheque, matching this exact mismatch. Irregular mandate, endorsement issues, and image-quality problems are all separate listed reasons for different defects, not a mismatch between account name and number.

questionBank.q: A customer's cheque has already been presented for clearing three times without success and is presented a fourth time. Under the approved reasons for returning cheques, what applies here?
opts: Wrong delivery
Presented more than 3 times
Multiple Presentation
Cheque Not Valid for Clearing
questionBank.exp: "Presented more than 3 times" is the specific listed reason matching a cheque that has already failed clearing on three prior occasions. "Multiple Presentation" is a separate listed reason covering a different pattern, while wrong delivery and general clearing invalidity are unrelated defects — the specific count-based reason is the one that fits a fourth presentation.

questionBank.q: A bank charges the beneficiary a fee for receiving an inward ACH credit. How is this treated under the listed abuses of the clearing process?
opts: It is a permitted practice as long as the fee is disclosed in advance
It is a listed abuse of the clearing process
It is permitted only for corporate beneficiaries
It is permitted if approved by the beneficiary's own bank
questionBank.exp: Banks charging beneficiaries for inward ACH credits is explicitly listed as an abuse of the clearing process that members are expected to avoid at all cost. Disclosure in advance, restricting it to corporate beneficiaries, or securing the beneficiary's bank's approval are not exceptions that make this practice acceptable — it's flagged as an abuse regardless.

questionBank.q: A bank refuses to pay a Manager's Cheque or Draft that it drew on itself. How is this treated under the listed abuses of the clearing process?
opts: It is acceptable if the bank cites insufficient liquidity
It is a listed abuse of the clearing process
It is acceptable if the instrument is more than 6 months old
It is acceptable only during a declared bank holiday
questionBank.exp: A bank refusing to pay its own instrument drawn on itself, such as a Manager's Cheque or Draft, is explicitly listed as an abuse of the clearing process. Citing liquidity concerns, instrument age, or a bank holiday are not recognized exceptions — refusing to honour one's own drawn instrument is treated as an abuse regardless of the stated reason.

questionBank.q: A customer of your bank deposits a cheque drawn on another bank into their account with you. From your bank's perspective, how is this cheque classified?
opts: Inward clearing cheque
Outward clearing cheque
Inward returned cheque
Special Caution Notice item
questionBank.exp: An Outward clearing cheque is defined as another bank's cheque lodged in your bank by your customer, for you to clear — exactly this scenario. Inward clearing describes the reverse situation (a cheque drawn on your bank, lodged elsewhere), inward returned describes a rejection scenario, and a Special Caution Notice is a distinct document type, not a cheque classification.

questionBank.q: A cheque drawn on your bank, which was lodged by a customer at another bank, is presented to you at the Clearing House for payment. How is this cheque classified from your bank's perspective?
opts: Outward clearing cheque
Inward clearing cheque
Outward returned cheque
A cheque requiring a Special Caution Notice by default
questionBank.exp: An Inward clearing cheque is defined as one drawn on your bank, lodged with another bank, that is subsequently presented to you for payment — exactly this scenario. Outward clearing describes the reverse case, outward returned describes a different rejection scenario, and a Special Caution Notice is only issued in specific delay circumstances, not by default on every inward cheque.

questionBank.q: In August 2007, what initiative did the CBN launch that eventually led to cheque truncation in Nigeria?
opts: The National Financial Inclusion Strategy
The Payments System Vision 2020 (PSV2020) Initiative
The Bank Verification Number project
The Cash-Lite Policy
questionBank.exp: CBN launched the Payments System Vision 2020 (PSV2020) Initiative in August 2007, intended to benchmark Nigeria's payments system against global best practices, which eventually led to cheque truncation. Financial inclusion strategy, the BVN project, and the Cash-Lite policy are all separate CBN initiatives with different aims and timelines.

questionBank.q: What does "Cheque Truncation" fundamentally mean, as defined in the process description?
opts: Physically shredding cheques after they clear
Converting a physical cheque into electronic form via scanned image for transmission
Reducing the maximum clearing amount for all cheques
Cancelling a cheque before it reaches the Clearing House
questionBank.exp: Cheque Truncation means conversion of a physical cheque into electronic form, by the collecting bank, through a scanned image transmitted to the Paying Bank — eliminating the cumbersome exchange of physical cheques. Shredding, reducing clearing amount limits, and outright cancellation are unrelated actions that don't capture what truncation actually does.

questionBank.q: What is the clearing demarcation timeline under the Cheque Truncation process, meaning when customers receive value?
opts: Same day (T+0)
questionBank.exp: Under the Cheque Truncation process, clearing demarcation is T+1, with the Revised Nigeria Bankers' Clearing System Rules 2018 specifying that customers receive value in the evening of T+1 by 10pm. Same-day value understates the actual timeline, while T+3 and T+7 both significantly overstate it.

questionBank.q: A branch wants to present a fresh cheque for clearing at the 2pm session. Is this permitted under the four clearing session rules?
opts: Yes, fresh cheques are accepted at all four sessions
No — the 2pm session only permits Returned cheques and NEFT items, not fresh cheques
Yes, but only if the cheque value is below N10 million
No, fresh cheques may only be presented after 5pm
questionBank.exp: The 2pm (Session 3) slot permits only Returned cheques, Fresh NEFT DR/CR, and Returned NEFT DR/CR — fresh cheques are explicitly not allowed at this session. They can, however, be presented at the earlier 8am or 11am sessions, so a value threshold (C) and a post-5pm-only rule (D) both misstate the actual restriction, which is about session timing, not cheque value or exclusivity to the last session.

questionBank.q: Under the Roles of Branches in the Cheque Truncation Process, how many times can a customer represent the same cheque?
opts: As many times as the customer wishes within the clearing window
Not more than twice
Exactly once, with no representation allowed at all
Up to five times, matching the "presented more than 3 times" return reason
questionBank.exp: Branches must ensure a customer cannot represent a cheque more than twice — a specific cap distinct from, though related to, the broader "presented more than 3 times" return reason that applies more generally across the clearing system. Unlimited representation, a single-attempt-only rule, and conflating this branch-level cap with the five-times figure in D all misstate the actual two-time limit branches are responsible for enforcing.

questionBank.q: An individual is found guilty of issuing a dishonoured cheque due to insufficient funds, under the Dishonoured Cheques Act 1977. What penalty applies to them?
opts: A fine of N5,000 with no imprisonment
Imprisonment for two years, without the option of a fine
A civil judgment for the cheque amount only
Community service for six months
questionBank.exp: For an individual found guilty under the Dishonoured Cheques Act 1977, the penalty is imprisonment for two years without the option of a fine — a criminal penalty, not merely a civil or monetary one. The N5,000 fine applies to corporate organizations instead, while a civil judgment alone or community service are not the penalties this Act specifies.

questionBank.q: CBN compiles information on serial issuers of dud cheques based on banks' returns. For how long are affected customers typically barred from the clearing system and from accessing credit facilities?
opts: 1 year
5 years
10 years
Permanently, with no time limit
questionBank.exp: Serial dud-cheque issuers are barred from the clearing system and from accessing credit facilities for a period of 5 years, and their names remain on credit bureau and CRMS databases for the same period. A 1-year bar understates the actual measure, 10 years overstates it, and a permanent bar misstates what is, per the CBN measures described, a defined 5-year period.

questionBank.q: A bank persistently transmits clearing data that does not agree with the corresponding cheque image. Per the clearing sanctions table, what is the consequence?
opts: A flat N50,000 fine per occurrence
N1,000 per item, with CBN reporting and suspension after 3 warnings
Immediate expulsion from the NBCH with no warning
The transaction is simply reversed with no further sanction
questionBank.exp: Persistent transmission of data not in agreement with the image attracts N1,000 per item, with the bank reported to CBN and suspended after 3 warnings. A flat N50,000 fine, immediate expulsion without warning, and a simple reversal with no sanction all misstate the graduated, per-item sanction actually specified.

questionBank.q: A paying bank processes payment on a cheque that had already been paid once before. Per the clearing sanctions table, who bears liability for this duplicated payment?
opts: The presenting bank, since it re-presented the cheque
The paying bank, which is fully liable for payment of duplicated cheques
Liability is split 50:50 between both banks
The customer, for depositing the cheque twice
questionBank.exp: Per the sanctions table, the paying bank shall be fully liable for payment of duplicated cheques — the paying bank is expected to catch and prevent a repeat payment. Assigning liability to the presenting bank, splitting it 50:50, or blaming the customer all misstate this specific sanction, which places full liability on the paying bank.

questionBank.q: A cheque presented for clearing has a postdated date, a stale date, and a mismatch between the amount in words and figures, and this irregularity leads to a fraud. Per the sanctions table, how is liability apportioned?
opts: The presenting bank alone bears full liability
The presenting and paying banks are jointly liable, 50:50
The paying bank alone bears full liability
Liability passes entirely to the CBN as regulator
questionBank.exp: Where clearing of cheques with irregularity (postdated, stale, or amount mismatch) leads to fraud, the presenting and paying banks shall be jointly liable, 50:50, reflecting shared responsibility for catching such defects before completing the transaction. Assigning full liability to only one bank, or to the CBN as regulator, misstates this specific joint-liability sanction.

questionBank.q: A bank presents a non-NUBAN transaction for clearing. Per the sanctions table, what is the consequence?
opts: Automatic suspension with no fine
N1,000 per transaction
A warning letter with no financial penalty
Full liability for any resulting loss, regardless of amount
questionBank.exp: Presenting non-NUBAN transactions for clearing attracts a sanction of N1,000 per transaction, per the sanctions table. Automatic suspension with no fine, a warning-only response, or an open-ended full-liability rule regardless of amount all overstate or misstate this specific, defined per-transaction fine.

questionBank.q: Treasury Operations (TROPS) is described as the "engine room" of a bank's Treasury function. What plays the equivalent "engine room" role for the Credit Department?
opts: Customer Service Unit (CSU)
Credit Operations (CROPs)
Cash and Teller Unit (CTU)
Internal Control
questionBank.exp: Treasury Operations is described as the engine room of Treasury, just as Credit Operations (CROPs) is the engine room of the Credit Department — a direct parallel drawn in the manual. CSU, CTU, and Internal Control serve entirely different functions and are not offered as the Credit Department's parallel processing unit.

questionBank.q: Although TROPS is a front office department, what relationship does it maintain with other departments in the bank?
opts: It operates in complete isolation, with no interaction with other departments
It has a direct relationship with other departments for the bank's funds management
It only interacts with the Cash & Teller Unit
It reports exclusively to the Foreign Operations department
questionBank.exp: Despite being a front office department, TROPS has a direct relationship with other departments for the funds management of the institution, and interacts with other banks for placements and takings. Complete isolation, limiting interaction to just the CTU, or exclusive reporting to Foreign Operations all misstate this cross-departmental relationship.

questionBank.q: Beyond processing transactions, what role does TROPS serve regarding documentation for Treasury Department activities?
opts: It has no documentation responsibility; that belongs to Internal Audit
It serves as the processing unit and custodian of all documents for Treasury activities
It only stores documents for foreign currency transactions
It forwards all documents to the CBN for storage
questionBank.exp: TROPS serves as the processing unit and custodian of all the documents for all the activities in the Treasury Department — a defined recordkeeping role, not one delegated elsewhere. Assigning this to Internal Audit, limiting it to only FCY documents, or forwarding everything to CBN all misstate this custodial responsibility.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as part of TROPS' functional breakdown, distinct from Settlement?
opts: Vault custody
Reconciliation
Teller supervision
Branch cash evacuation
questionBank.exp: Reconciliation is listed as one of TROPS' functions, alongside records/book-keeping, documentation, confirmation, verification, and settlement. Vault custody, teller supervision, and branch cash evacuation are Cash & Teller Unit functions, not part of the TROPS functional breakdown.

questionBank.q: CBN's statement of account shows a debit related to a Cash Reserve Requirement (CRR) adjustment. Which unit is responsible for raising the entries for this?
opts: Cash & Teller Unit
TROPS
Customer Service Unit
Foreign Operations
questionBank.exp: TROPS is responsible for raising entries for CBN Direct Debits and Credits, which include Cash Reserve Requirement adjustments noted in CBN account statements. The CTU, CSU, and Foreign Operations are not the units tasked with raising entries for this specific CBN-driven transaction type.

questionBank.q: A bank without a branch in a particular location appoints another local bank with a branch there to render services to its customers. What is this arrangement called?
opts: Correspondent Banking Agreement
Domestic Correspondence Banking Service (DCBS)
Cash Sweep Arrangement
Agency Clearing Arrangement
questionBank.exp: This exact arrangement is defined as Domestic Correspondence Banking Service (DCBS) — interaction between two local banks where one appoints another as its representative in a location it lacks a branch. "Correspondent Banking Agreement" and "Agency Clearing Arrangement" are plausible-sounding but not the actual term used, and Cash Sweep is an unrelated vault-deposit service.

questionBank.q: Before a bank can rely on another local bank's branch to render services under DCBS, what must be in place between the two banks?
opts: A joint venture agreement registered with the CBN
A Service Level Agreement (SLA)
A merger clearance from the SEC
A shared banking license
questionBank.exp: There must be a Service Level Agreement (SLA) between the two banks for DCBS to operate. A registered joint venture, SEC merger clearance, or a shared license are not the mechanism described — an SLA is the specific documented arrangement required.

questionBank.q: A bank wants to pool funds from several individual investors to meet the CBN's minimum purchase sum for Treasury Bills. What is that minimum figure?
opts: N5 million
N50 million
N500 million
N5 billion
questionBank.exp: CBN's guideline permits banks to pool funds from individuals to make up the minimum Treasury Bills purchase sum of N50 million. N5 million understates the figure by a factor of ten, while N500 million and N5 billion both significantly overstate it.

questionBank.q: For a Bankers Acceptance (BA), the bank is the primary obligor. How is this reflected in the bank's accounting treatment, compared to a Commercial Paper (CP) where the customer is the primary obligor?
opts: Both BA and CP values are recorded on the balance sheet identically
The BA value is recorded on the balance sheet, while the CP's aggregate value is treated as an off-balance-sheet item
The BA value is off-balance-sheet, while CP is recorded on the balance sheet
Neither instrument appears on the bank's books under any circumstance
questionBank.exp: Because the bank is the primary obligor for a BA, its value is recorded on the balance sheet; for a CP, the customer is the primary obligor, so the aggregate value is treated as an off-balance-sheet item instead. Treating both identically, reversing the treatment, or excluding both from the books entirely all misstate this obligor-driven accounting distinction.

questionBank.q: A Commercial Paper (CP) is ordinarily unsecured. What happens when a bank adds its own guarantee to a CP?
opts: It becomes ineligible for CBN's 150% equity cap calculation
It becomes a Guaranteed Commercial Paper (GCP)
It automatically converts into a Bankers Acceptance
It must then be recorded exclusively off the balance sheet with no exceptions
questionBank.exp: When a bank adds its guarantee to a Commercial Paper, the CP becomes a Guaranteed Commercial Paper (GCP) — a distinct labeled category, though still governed by the same 150% equity cap alongside BAs. It doesn't become exempt from the cap calculation, doesn't convert into a BA, and its off-balance-sheet treatment as a CP doesn't change simply by being guaranteed.

questionBank.q: Per CBN rules, what combined ceiling applies to a bank's Bankers Acceptances (BA) and Commercial Papers (CP) together?
opts: 50% of the Equity Capital of the bank
150% of the Equity Capital of the bank
300% of the Equity Capital of the bank
There is no ceiling; only reporting is required
questionBank.exp: The CBN rule caps both BA and CP together at not more than 150% of the Equity Capital of a bank. 50% and 300% both misstate the actual figure, and claiming there's no ceiling at all directly contradicts the stated rule.

questionBank.q: A customer wants to purchase foreign currency from the bank through the Bureau De Change channel. Under which Treasury Product category does this fall?
opts: Local Currency Investment Products
Foreign Currency Products
BAs and CPs
Domestic Correspondence Banking Service
questionBank.exp: Sales to Bureau De Change (BDC) is specifically listed under Foreign Currency Treasury Products, alongside customer FX sales, interbank FX trades, and FX transfers. Local Currency Investment Products, BAs/CPs, and DCBS are entirely separate categories that don't cover FX/BDC transactions.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as an example of an Interbank FX trade under Treasury's Foreign Currency Products?
opts: Treasury Bills secondary market trading
Spots, forwards, and SWAPS
Certificates of Deposit purchases
FGN and State Bonds trading
questionBank.exp: Spots, forwards, and SWAPS are the listed examples of Interbank FX trades under Foreign Currency Products. Treasury Bills, Certificates of Deposit, and FGN/State Bonds trading are all listed instead under Local Currency Investment Products, not FX trades.

questionBank.q: Which source document, coming from Treasury Dealers, contains the dealer's name, deal date, amount, and maturity date?
opts: Cash Lodgment Slip
Deal Slip
Foreign Exchange Deal Slip
Debit Note
questionBank.exp: The Deal Slip is the source document from Treasury Dealers that specifically contains dealer name, date, amount, and maturity date. A Cash Lodgment Slip records deposits from the Treasury Department, a Foreign Exchange Deal Slip is a separate, FX-specific version from the FX Department, and a Debit Note is a different clearing-related instrument entirely.

questionBank.q: CBN Debits and Credits appear in a bank's statement of account. In what form do these arrive at TROPS, and what must TROPS do with them?
opts: They arrive as verbal instructions, and TROPS logs them without further action
They arrive as statements from CBN, and TROPS must raise entries for them
They arrive pre-posted, requiring no action from TROPS
They arrive only once a month for batch processing
questionBank.exp: CBN Debits and Credits come in the form of statements from CBN, and TROPS must raise entries for them — an active processing task, not passive logging. Verbal-only instructions, pre-posted entries needing no action, and a monthly-only batch cycle all misstate how these statements are received and handled.

questionBank.q: Which platform is described as a CBN system where transfer of money between banks takes place on a real-time and gross basis?
opts: SWIFT
RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement)
Flexcube
Bloomberg
questionBank.exp: RTGS is specifically defined as the CBN system where transfer of money from one bank to another takes place on a real-time and gross basis. SWIFT is used for FX processing and settlement between correspondent banks, Flexcube is a bank's core banking software, and Bloomberg is listed only generically as another market platform — none is defined as this specific real-time gross settlement system.

questionBank.q: CIFTS, now known as NISS, is described as an integral part of which broader system, used to process huge funds transfers between banks?
opts: SWIFT
RTGS
Flexcube
DCBS
questionBank.exp: CIFTS (now NISS) is described as an integral part of RTGS, used to process huge funds transfers between banks. It is not part of SWIFT (a separate FX-focused platform), Flexcube (a bank's own core banking software), or DCBS (an interbank service arrangement, not a settlement system).

questionBank.q: What is described as the major advantage of the SWIFT platform, used for processing foreign currency transactions between correspondent banks?
opts: Speed of settlement above all else
Security
Zero transaction cost
Automatic currency conversion
questionBank.exp: Security is specifically named as SWIFT's major advantage, given its role in processing foreign currency transactions and settlements between correspondent banks. Speed, zero cost, and automatic conversion are not the advantage highlighted for this platform in the module.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is given as an example of a bank's Core Banking Package, as distinct from a settlement platform like RTGS?
opts: NISS
Flexcube
CIFTS
SWIFT
questionBank.exp: Flexcube is given as an example of a bank's Core Banking Package, alongside Basis and Finacle — the software a bank selects for its entire operation. NISS, CIFTS, and SWIFT are all settlement or funds-transfer platforms rather than a bank's own core banking software.

questionBank.q: A TROPS officer receives a deal slip from Treasury. Before processing, what must the officer verify about the slip itself?
opts: That it was submitted electronically rather than on paper
That it is time-stamped and signed by two dealers
That it was countersigned by the branch manager
That it references at least two counterparties
questionBank.exp: The TROPS officer vets the deal slip specifically to ensure it is time-stamped and signed by two dealers, a dual-authorization check before any processing begins. Electronic-only submission, branch manager countersignature, and multi-counterparty referencing are not the checks the procedure specifies.

questionBank.q: A counterparty in a deal does not have a placement line with the bank, or has exceeded its approved line. What must the TROPS officer do?
opts: Process the transaction anyway, since deal slips are self-authorizing
Return the deal slip to the dealer, unless the credit committee has approved it
Automatically escalate to the CBN for a special exemption
Split the transaction into smaller tranches to stay within the line
questionBank.exp: Where the counterparty lacks a placement line or has exceeded it, the TROPS officer returns the deal slip to the dealer, except where the credit committee has approved it — this is the one recognized override. Processing anyway, escalating to the CBN, or splitting the transaction into smaller tranches are not sanctioned workarounds around a missing or exceeded placement line.

questionBank.q: After a TROPS officer posts the details on a deal slip and transmits funds to the counterparty, what must the Head of TROPS still do?
opts: Nothing further; the officer's action completes the transaction
Approve all transactions and generate an electronic copy and covering letter
Personally deliver the letter to CBN
Re-vet the original deal slip for dealer signatures a second time
questionBank.exp: The Head of TROPS approves all transactions and generates the electronic copy and covering letter — a required managerial sign-off after the officer's processing steps. Treating the officer's posting as final with no further step, personally delivering to CBN (a runner's task), or re-vetting signatures a second time are not part of this required approval step.

questionBank.q: For an Open Buy Back (OBB) transaction, what does the procedure specifically require the TROPS officer to prepare?
opts: A Special Caution Notice
A letter to the Discount Office, CBN
A letter to the Nigerian Bankers' Clearing House
A Certificate of Capital Importation
questionBank.exp: For OBB transactions, the officer prepares a letter to the Discount Office, CBN, which a TROPS runner then delivers and returns with an acknowledged copy. A Special Caution Notice belongs to the clearing process, an NBCH letter is unrelated to OBB processing, and a Certificate of Capital Importation belongs to foreign capital transactions, not OBB deals.

questionBank.q: According to TROPS Operations Policies, what should the unit's Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) specifically include, alongside the organization chart?
opts: A list of all customer names with active accounts
Authorization limits and risk acceptance criteria to guide processing compliance
The bank's full annual financial statements
A copy of every deal slip processed in the prior year
questionBank.exp: The SOP should specifically contain, among other things, authorization limits and risk acceptance criteria to guide processing compliance, alongside roles, schedules, and mandates. Customer name lists, annual financial statements, and archives of prior deal slips are not listed as required SOP contents.

questionBank.q: A single staff member in TROPS both initiates a transaction and also confirms and records it, with no other staff involved. What internal control principle does this violate?
opts: Written Mandates
Segregation of Duties
Confirmation stage requirements
Authorization Limits
questionBank.exp: Segregation of Duties requires that one person must not be allowed to initiate a transaction and conclude it — initiation, confirmation, recording, and settlement should be handled separately. Written Mandates concerns instructions being documented rather than verbal, Confirmation stage requirements concern the pre-processing check itself, and Authorization Limits concerns figure-based caps — none is the specific principle a single person doing everything violates.

questionBank.q: The staff member who prepares a source document in TROPS also approves and authorizes its posting. What internal control does this breach?
opts: Passwords should be tied to authorization limits
The preparer of a source document should not be the one to approve or authorize its posting
All TROPS transactions require a confirmation stage
All instructions or mandates must be in writing
questionBank.exp: Authorization control specifically requires that the staff preparing the source document should not be the one to approve or authorize its posting — a distinct check from segregation of duties more broadly. Password-limit tying, confirmation-stage requirements, and written-mandate rules are separate controls that don't describe this specific preparer/approver conflict.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a category covered under TROPS' Authorization Limits?
opts: The number of deal slips a dealer may submit per day
The amount a Junior or Senior Dealer can handle
The number of hours a TROPS officer may work per week
The size of the bank's overall loan book
questionBank.exp: Amounts that Junior or Senior Dealers can handle is one of the specific categories listed under Authorization Limits, alongside signatory approval amounts and posting limits by officer category. Daily submission counts, working hours, and the bank's overall loan book size are not among the listed authorization-limit categories.

questionBank.q: A senior manager gives a TROPS staff member a verbal instruction to process an unusual transaction, without any written confirmation. What does the internal control on Written Mandates say about this?
opts: It is permitted as long as the manager holds a senior enough title
All instructions must be in writing; verbal instructions, even from top Management, should not be implemented
It is permitted if a witness confirms the instruction verbally
It is permitted for transactions below the officer's authorization limit
questionBank.exp: The Written Mandates control explicitly states that all instructions or mandates must be in writing, and staff should not implement verbal instructions even from top Management, since verbal instructions can be denied. Seniority of the instructing manager, a verbal witness, or the transaction falling under an authorization limit are not exceptions this control recognizes.

questionBank.q: A bank receives repayment of a Commercial Paper investment, including accrued interest. How is this classified under TROPS' sample processing categories?
opts: Outflow
Inflow
Open Buy Back settlement
Cash Reserve Requirement adjustment
questionBank.exp: Repayment of investment in Commercial Paper (CP) or Bankers Acceptances (BA), including fees, interests, or discount, is listed under Inflow. Outflow describes the opposite direction (payments the bank makes out), an OBB settlement is a distinct transaction type of its own, and a CRR adjustment is a separate CBN-driven entry category.

questionBank.q: A bank makes a payment to another bank on behalf of a third party. How is this classified under TROPS' sample processing categories?
opts: Inflow
Outflow
Fixed Buy Back settlement
Domestic Correspondence Banking Service fee
questionBank.exp: Payment to other banks on behalf of a third party is listed under Outflow — funds leaving the bank. Inflow describes the opposite direction, FBB settlement is a distinct secured-placement transaction type, and a DCBS fee is unrelated to this specific third-party payment scenario.

questionBank.q: A counterparty enters into an Open Buy Back (OBB) arrangement rather than a Fixed Buy Back (FBB). What key flexibility distinguishes OBB from FBB?
opts: OBB requires no Treasury Bills as security, unlike FBB
OBB allows the counterparty or bank to call for its deposit at any time, unlike FBB which runs for a fixed period
OBB is only available to government agencies, unlike FBB
OBB has no maximum tenor, while FBB is capped at 91 days
questionBank.exp: OBB's defining flexibility is that the counterparty or the bank can call for its deposit at any time, whereas FBB runs for a fixed period during which the counterparty cannot call for the deposit early. Both OBB and FBB are secured by Treasury Bills (so A is wrong), neither is restricted to government agencies, and it's OBB — not FBB — that has the flexible timing (as short as 1 day or as long as 91 days), so D misstates which instrument has which constraint.

questionBank.q: Per the Transaction Processing Checklist, what must be true of all accounts before a TROPS officer proceeds with processing?
opts: All accounts must have been opened within the last 12 months
All accounts must be funded
All accounts must belong to corporate customers only
All accounts must have a zero balance at start of day
questionBank.exp: The checklist requires that all accounts must be funded before processing — a basic pre-condition for any transaction to proceed. A 12-month account-age requirement, corporate-only restriction, and a zero-starting-balance rule are not conditions this checklist specifies.

questionBank.q: What is the Treasury Single Account (TSA), as defined in the module?
opts: A private banking product offered to high-net-worth government officials
A public accounting system where all government revenue and payments are collected into and paid from one single account
A special interbank clearing account used only during cheque truncation
A joint account maintained by all commercial banks for shared liquidity
questionBank.exp: TSA is defined as a public accounting system under which all government revenue, receipts, and income are collected into one single account, usually maintained by the Central Bank, with all payments also done through this account. A private banking product for officials, a cheque-truncation-specific account, and a shared interbank liquidity account all misstate this public accounting concept.

questionBank.q: Which constitutional provision requires that all revenues and expenditure of the federation be paid into and from a Consolidated Revenue Fund?
opts: Section 47 of the CBN Act
Section 80(1) of the 1999 Constitution as amended
Section 12(1) of BOFIA
Section 61 of the Companies and Allied Matters Act
questionBank.exp: Section 80(1) of the 1999 Constitution as amended is the specific provision requiring all federation revenues and expenditure to flow through a Consolidated Revenue Fund. The CBN Act, BOFIA, and CAMA are real statutes governing other areas of banking, not the constitutional basis for this specific revenue-consolidation requirement.

questionBank.q: Under TSA's operational modalities, what happens to the accounts Ministries, Departments, and Agencies (MDAs) hold with commercial banks at the end of each banking day?
opts: They accrue interest overnight before being remitted the next morning
They must be zeroized, as all monies are remitted to the Consolidated Revenue Account with CBN
They are frozen until month-end reconciliation is complete
They are consolidated into a single commercial bank of the government's choosing
questionBank.exp: MDA accounts with commercial banks must be zeroized at the end of every banking day, since commercial banks are mandated to remit all monies to the Consolidated Revenue Account with CBN daily — this is also why banks no longer have access to the float these accounts once provided. Overnight interest accrual, month-end freezing, and consolidation into one chosen commercial bank all misstate this daily zeroization requirement.

questionBank.q: What is identified as a key benefit of the Treasury Single Account, beyond accountability and transparency?
opts: It increases the float commercial banks can access from MDA accounts
It helps ensure proper cash management by eliminating idle funds left with different commercial banks
It eliminates the need for any government auditing of revenue collection
It allows MDAs to independently choose which bank holds their funds long-term
questionBank.exp: A key TSA benefit is helping ensure proper cash management by eliminating idle funds usually left scattered across different commercial banks, and enhancing reconciliation of revenue collection and payment. It does the opposite of increasing bank float access (A), doesn't eliminate auditing (C), and removes rather than preserves MDA discretion over which bank holds funds long-term (D).

questionBank.q: The module's conclusion notes that TROPS functions must remain distinct from the front office and middle office, operating in "water-tight compartments." What is the purpose of this separation?
opts: To reduce the total number of staff required in Treasury overall
To ensure satisfactory adherence to the bank's policy and procedures
To allow TROPS to bypass CBN reporting requirements
To eliminate the need for any SLA between departments
questionBank.exp: The water-tight compartmentalization between TROPS, front office, and middle office is meant to ensure satisfactory adherence to policy and procedures — essentially an operational control against conflicts of interest across functions. It's not framed as a staffing-reduction measure, doesn't allow bypassing CBN reporting, and doesn't eliminate the need for SLAs governing other interbank arrangements like DCBS.

questionBank.q: How is Funds Transfer described in relation to a bank's financial system?
opts: A regulatory requirement with no direct benefit to the bank
A service leveraging the bank's financial system for effective transfer and settlement
A backup process used only when RTGS is unavailable
A manual process that bypasses the bank's core system entirely
questionBank.exp: Funds Transfer is described as a service the bank gives customers, leveraging the bank's financial system for effective and efficient transfer and settlement. It is not framed as a mere regulatory obligation, a fallback for RTGS outages, or a manual bypass of the core system — it's a core, system-integrated service.

questionBank.q: What is the Funds Transfer Unit (FTU), as defined in the module?
opts: The unit that manages the bank's physical vault operations
The section handling remittance or settlement of obligations between banks or on behalf of customers
The unit responsible for clearing physical cheques only
The unit that approves new account openings
questionBank.exp: The FTU is defined as the section of a bank where funds remittance or settlement of obligations between banks, or on behalf of customers, is carried out. Vault operations, cheque clearing specifically, and account-opening approval are all handled by other named units, not the FTU.

questionBank.q: While funds transfer involves the actual movement of funds, what may a settlement system additionally include?
opts: Only cash withdrawals from an ATM network
A set-off of obligations or, in some cases, countertrade arrangements
Only foreign currency conversion at spot rates
Only the printing of physical bank drafts
questionBank.exp: A settlement system may additionally include a set-off of obligations or, in some cases, countertrade arrangements — a broader concept than the literal transfer of funds itself. ATM cash withdrawals, spot FX conversion, and draft printing are unrelated operational activities, not the distinguishing feature the module draws between funds transfer and settlement.

questionBank.q: From the customer's perspective, which of the following is listed as a rationale for using funds transfer instead of carrying physical cash?
opts: It increases the risk of loss compared to cash
Reduction in risks arising from carrying cash
It is generally slower than physical cash delivery
It requires more documentation than a cash transaction
questionBank.exp: Reduction in risks arising from carrying cash is explicitly listed as a customer-perspective rationale, alongside convenience, security, speed, and cost efficiency. Increased risk, slower delivery, and heavier documentation all contradict the benefits actually listed for customers choosing funds transfer over cash.

questionBank.q: From the bank's perspective, what does funds transfer serve as a source of, beyond customer convenience?
opts: A source of regulatory penalties to be minimized
A source of fee or float income
A source of increased cash-holding costs
A source of additional teller staffing requirements
questionBank.exp: From the bank's perspective, funds transfer is listed as a source of cheap/low-cost funds and fee/float income, alongside cross-selling opportunities and growing the customer base. Regulatory penalties, increased cash-holding costs, and added teller staffing needs are not among the listed bank-side benefits.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the Funds Transfer Functions, alongside processing drafts and manager's cheques?
opts: Vault compartment dual-key custody
Executing customers' Standing Orders
Cheque truncation image scanning
Teller cash evacuation to the vault
questionBank.exp: Executing customers' Standing Orders is explicitly listed among the Funds Transfer Functions, alongside CBN and NIBSS transfers, electronic and in-house transfers, and processing transfer mandates. Vault custody, cheque truncation scanning, and teller cash evacuation are Cash & Teller Unit or clearing-process activities, not FTU functions.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a common Local Funds Transfer method, distinct from cheques, drafts, or RTGS?
opts: Cheque truncation clearing sessions
Funds Transfer using Mobile Phones
Special Caution Notice issuance
Vault-In Register entries
questionBank.exp: Funds Transfer using Mobile Phones is explicitly listed as a common Local FT method, alongside account-to-account transfers, cheques/drafts, CBN RTGS, NIBSS-NEFT, mail transfer, and in-house clearing. Truncation sessions, Special Caution Notices, and Vault-In Register entries belong to the clearing and cash-operations processes, not the list of local FT methods.

questionBank.q: Approximately what share of routine banking transactions does funds transfer account for, per the module?
opts: Less than 10%
More than 50%
Exactly 25%
Nearly 100%, with cash transactions being negligible
questionBank.exp: The module states that funds transfer accounts for more than 50% of routine banking transactions. Under 10% and exactly 25% both significantly understate this share, while claiming cash transactions are negligible overstates the point being made — the figure given is "more than 50%," not near-total dominance.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is named as an International Model FT System among the Foreign Funds Transfer methods listed?
opts: NIBSS Instant Payment (NIP)
Western Union
NIBSS Automated Payment System (NAPS)
Mobile Money
questionBank.exp: Western Union is specifically named as an International Model FT System under Foreign Funds Transfer methods, alongside travelers' cheques, domiciliary account inflows, foreign bank drafts, and mail transfer. NIP, NAPS, and Mobile Money are domestic NIBSS or bank-driven products, not the named international system.

questionBank.q: Under Foreign Funds Transfer methods, how is a Mail Transfer specifically defined?
opts: An electronic message sent through SWIFT to a domestic bank
A written order to a foreign correspondent bank to pay locally
A physical courier delivery of cash between two countries
A verbal instruction confirmed later by telephone
questionBank.exp: Mail Transfer, under Foreign FT methods, is defined as an order in writing addressed to a foreign correspondent bank to pay on behalf of a local bank. It is not an electronic SWIFT message, a physical cash courier, or a verbal instruction — the defining feature is that it's a written order to a correspondent bank.

questionBank.q: A funds transfer transaction is jointly processed by the Sender's Bank and the Beneficiary's Bank through a third party such as CBN, NIBSS, or a Discount House. What role does this third party play among the Parties to FT?
opts: Remitter
Intermediary
Beneficiary
Beneficiary's Bank
questionBank.exp: The Intermediary — which may be CBN, NIBSS, or Discount Houses — is the party mutually shared by the Sender Bank and Beneficiary's Bank to facilitate the transfer. Remitter, Beneficiary, and Beneficiary's Bank are the other named parties, each describing a different role in the transaction, not the shared facilitating third party.

questionBank.q: How does the module define "settlement," as distinct from the payment system itself?
opts: The physical printing and delivery of a bank draft
The execution of payment instructions received, which may include settlement of securities, FX, or derivatives
The act of a customer signing a funds transfer application form
The reconciliation of a teller's daily cash proof sheet
questionBank.exp: Settlement is defined as the execution of payment instructions received, which may include settlement of securities, foreign exchange, or derivatives transactions — a broader concept than the payment system, which is simply the process of transferring value between a payer and beneficiary. Draft printing, form signing, and teller proof reconciliation are unrelated activities, not this specific definitional distinction.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the stated objectives of any settlement system?
opts: Maximum profitability for the settling bank
Safety, security, soundness, effectiveness, and efficiency
Minimizing the number of participating banks
Eliminating the need for any CBN oversight
questionBank.exp: Safety, security, soundness, effectiveness, and efficiency are the objectives explicitly listed for any settlement system. Maximizing bank profitability, minimizing participant numbers, or eliminating CBN oversight are not among these stated objectives — the goals listed are systemic and prudential, not bank-specific or deregulatory.

questionBank.q: A payment is made using a paper instrument like a cheque or dividend warrant, and its value is not immediately available since it must first clear. Under the Classification of Payments and Settlement Systems, which category does this fall under?
opts: Electronic Payment System
Traditional Payment System
Wholesale Payment System
Retail Payment System
questionBank.exp: The Traditional Payment System specifically involves cash and paper instruments like cheques, drafts, and warrants, where value is not immediate because such instruments must be cleared. Electronic systems use devices like phones, computers, and ATMs for faster processing, while Wholesale and Retail are sub-categories of the Electronic system, not the paper-based one this scenario describes.

questionBank.q: A large funds transfer takes place between two banks through SWIFT, entirely separate from any individual customer's retail transaction. Under the Electronic Payment System classification, which category does this fall under?
opts: Retail Payment Systems
Wholesale Payment Systems
Traditional Payment Systems
Mobile Money Systems
questionBank.exp: Wholesale Payment Systems (electronic) handle transactions between banks, governments, and other financial organizations, done through platforms like SWIFT and NIBSS (NEFT) — matching this interbank scenario exactly. Retail Payment Systems instead cover customer transactions via smart cards, ATMs, and phone banking, Traditional systems are paper-based, and Mobile Money is a specific retail product, not this interbank category.

questionBank.q: How is Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) defined in terms of when and how transfers are executed?
opts: A system where small transfers are batched and processed once daily
A system executing large fund transfers on a real-time, gross basis
A manual paper-based process requiring physical bank drafts
A system exclusively for foreign currency conversions
questionBank.exp: RTGS is defined as a settlement system where transfer of large funds or securities is executed between one bank and another on a "real time" and "gross" basis. Batched daily processing describes net settlement systems like NEFT instead, RTGS is electronic rather than paper-based, and it is not exclusive to foreign currency conversion — it handles various high-value Naira and settlement transactions.

questionBank.q: What does "gross" settlement specifically mean in the context of RTGS?
opts: Transactions are bunched together and netted against each other before settling
Each transaction is settled on a one-to-one basis, and once processed, is final and irrevocable
Only transactions above a set threshold are settled at all
Settlement only happens once at the end of each business week
questionBank.exp: Gross settlement means the transaction is settled on a one-to-one basis without bunching or netting with any other transaction; once processed, payments are final and irrevocable. Netting/bunching describes net settlement (the opposite of gross), a threshold-only rule and weekly-only settlement are not features described for RTGS gross settlement.

questionBank.q: The software originally known as CBN Interbank Funds Transfer (CIFT), which processes funds transfers on RTGS, has since been renamed to what?
opts: NIBSS Electronic Funds Transfer (NEFT)
Nigeria Settlement System (NISS)
NIBSS Instant Payment (NIP)
NIBSS Automated Payment System (NAPS)
questionBank.exp: CIFT has been renamed the Nigeria Settlement System (NISS), the software that processes RTGS transfers today. NEFT, NIP, and NAPS are all separate, distinct NIBSS products with their own functions, not the renamed version of CIFT.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed among the stated Goals of RTGS?
opts: To increase settlement lag for better auditability
To reduce settlement risk due to settlement lag
To phase out high-value payments in favor of retail transfers
To eliminate the need for participating banks to hold settlement accounts
questionBank.exp: Reducing settlement risk due to settlement lag is one of the explicitly listed Goals of RTGS, alongside reducing credit risk, speeding up high-value payments, and giving an accurate position of the participating bank. Increasing settlement lag, phasing out high-value payments, or eliminating settlement accounts all contradict RTGS's actual stated goals and design (RTGS requires settlement accounts with CBN).

questionBank.q: How does RTGS's typical transaction value compare with that of NEFT?
opts: RTGS and NEFT handle identical transaction value ranges
RTGS focuses mainly on high value, NEFT generally on smaller value
RTGS is reserved exclusively for retail customers, while NEFT serves only corporates
NEFT handles higher value transactions than RTGS in all cases
questionBank.exp: RTGS is designed mainly to focus on high value transactions, while NEFT's system is generally for smaller value transactions — this is one of the explicit differences drawn between the two. Claiming identical ranges, reversing the retail/corporate framing (neither system is defined by customer type), or reversing which system handles higher values all misstate the actual comparison.

questionBank.q: Since when has RTGS been running on the SWIFT (Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication) network?
opts: January 1, 2004
September 4, 2014
February 2, 2015
April 1, 2021
questionBank.exp: RTGS has been running on the SWIFT network since September 4, 2014. January 2004 relates instead to NEFT's introduction, February 2, 2015 relates to NAPS' launch, and April 1, 2021 relates to the new Nigeria Cheque Standard's full operation — each a different date tied to a different system.

questionBank.q: In the RTGS (NISS) Processing steps, what does the bank do to the remitter's account after verifying the completed application and signature?
opts: Credit the remitter's account with the transfer amount plus charges
Debit the remitter's account for the amount to be transferred plus charges
Freeze the remitter's account pending CBN clearance
Transfer the account to a dormant status until confirmation
questionBank.exp: After verification, the procedure debits the remitter's account for the amount to be transferred plus charges, before crediting the Designated Account and processing the RTGS platform entry. Crediting the remitter (the reverse direction), freezing the account, or making it dormant are not steps in this processing sequence.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as an example of a High Value RTGS payment under "Settlement of High Value Payment"?
opts: Payment of a customer's monthly utility bill
Interbank Takings and Interbank Placements
A single NEFT transfer for club subscription fees
A Mobile Money airtime purchase
questionBank.exp: Interbank Takings and Interbank Placements are listed as examples under Settlement of High Value Payment via RTGS, alongside FX purchases/sales and Treasury Bills purchases/sales. Utility bill payments, club subscription NEFT transfers, and Mobile Money airtime purchases are all lower-value retail transactions handled by other systems, not RTGS high-value settlement.

questionBank.q: How is NIBSS (Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System) described in terms of its ownership and the CBN's role?
opts: NIBSS is wholly owned and operated by the CBN directly
NIBSS is owned by Banks and Discount Houses; CBN only supervises
NIBSS is a private company with no regulatory oversight from the CBN
NIBSS is jointly owned by the CBN and foreign correspondent banks
questionBank.exp: NIBSS is a body established and owned by Banks and Discount Houses, with the CBN acting only as a supervisory body that appoints the Chairman of the board — it is not CBN-owned outright, unregulated, or foreign-owned. This ownership structure is distinct from RTGS, which is a CBN initiative in its own right.

questionBank.q: A bank wants to transfer N100 million through NIBSS, secured by its Treasury Bills pledged to NIBSS. At minimum, how much T/Bills coverage must the bank hold at NIBSS before the transfer can be affected?
opts: Exactly N100 million (100% coverage)
At least N110 million (110% coverage)
At least N150 million (150% coverage)
No T/Bills coverage is required for NIBSS transfers
questionBank.exp: The originating bank's T/Bills holding at NIBSS must cover the amount to be transferred by at least 110% before the transfer can be affected — so for a N100 million transfer, at least N110 million in pledged T/Bills is required. Exact 100% coverage understates the required buffer, 150% overstates it, and claiming no coverage is required directly contradicts the rule that all NIBSS transactions are secured by pledged T/Bills.

questionBank.q: A NIBSS transfer is completed on a Wednesday. When does the beneficiary typically receive value for this transaction?
opts: The following Monday, after weekly batch processing
Same day's value
T+1, the following business day
Only after a 48-hour security hold
questionBank.exp: All NIBSS transfers have the same day's value — completed transactions settle the same day they're processed. A weekly batch delay, a T+1 timeline, or a 48-hour hold all misstate this same-day value rule, which is one of NIBSS's defining features.

questionBank.q: Which of the following institutions is listed as relying on NIBSS for the settlement of its operations?
opts: The Nigerian Bankers' Clearing House exclusively
Central Securities Clearing System Limited (CSCS)
The Federal Ministry of Finance
The National Assembly Budget Office
questionBank.exp: Central Securities Clearing System Limited (CSCS) is explicitly listed among institutions relying on NIBSS for settlement, alongside all Settlement/Clearing Banks and private switching companies like Interswitch. The NBCH, Ministry of Finance, and Budget Office are not among the institutions specifically listed as relying on NIBSS in this section.

questionBank.q: NEFT was introduced in Nigeria to provide electronic payment options for consumers, banks, governments and organizations. In what year was it introduced?
questionBank.exp: NEFT was introduced in Nigeria in March 2004. 2010 doesn't correspond to any named milestone in this module, 2015 relates instead to NAPS' launch, and 2021 relates to the new Nigeria Cheque Standard's full operation — each a distinct system with its own timeline.

questionBank.q: Why is a NEFT payment described as an irrevocable fund transfer instruction?
opts: Because NEFT transfers cannot be reversed even in cases of proven fraud
Because the payer's bank won't accept the order if funds are insufficient
Because NEFT operates only through a single designated bank nationwide
Because NEFT instructions must be notarized before submission
questionBank.exp: NEFT is irrevocable specifically because the payer's bank simply will not accept the order if there are insufficient funds to cover the payment instruction — the funding check happens up front, so a validly accepted instruction can't later fail for lack of funds. A blanket no-fraud-reversal claim, single-bank-only operation, and a notarization requirement are not the basis given for NEFT's irrevocability.

questionBank.q: A company processes its monthly staff salaries as a single electronic file submitted through a clearing bank. Under NEFT's variants, how is this classified?
opts: Single Item NEFT
Bulk NEFT
NIBSS Instant Payment (NIP)
A Bank's Own Dedicated Instant Payment
questionBank.exp: Bulk NEFT involves several NEFT instructions presented in an electronic file through a clearing bank — salary payments are given as a specific example. Single Item NEFT covers individual instructions like club subscriptions or utility payments, NIP is a separate real-time person-to-bank product, and a bank's own dedicated system is a different, internally-developed product entirely.

questionBank.q: An insurance company collects premium payments from policyholders through automated direct debits, based on the policyholders' pre-authorized instructions. Under Bulk NEFT, how is this classified?
opts: Bulk NEFT Credits
Bulk NEFT Debits
Single Item NEFT
NIBSS Automated Payment System (NAPS)
questionBank.exp: Bulk NEFT Debits are Automated Direct Debits such as insurance premium payments, scheduled donations, and utility bill payments, based on payers' pre-authorized instructions — matching this exact scenario. Bulk NEFT Credits instead describes salaries, pensions, and dividends flowing outward to recipients, Single Item NEFT covers individual instructions rather than bulk files, and NAPS is a related but separate bulk-payment product.

questionBank.q: Comparing RTGS and NEFT settlement styles, how is NEFT specifically classified?
opts: Gross settlement, identical to RTGS
Deferred Net Basis (DNS), where transactions complete in batches at specific times
Real-time push settlement with no batching at all
A settlement style used only for foreign currency transfers
questionBank.exp: NEFT is based on net-settlement, specifically Deferred Net Basis (DNS), where transactions are completed in batches at specific times — the direct opposite of RTGS's one-to-one gross settlement. Claiming it's identical to RTGS's gross settlement, calling it real-time push with no batching, or restricting it to FX transfers all misstate NEFT's actual batched, net-settlement design.

questionBank.q: What key feature distinguishes NIBSS Instant Payment (NIP) from standard NEFT transfers in terms of availability and speed?
opts: NIP is available only during standard banking hours, like NEFT
NIP is available 24/7 for instant transfer to another bank
NIP requires a physical branch visit for every transaction
NIP is limited exclusively to government revenue collection
questionBank.exp: NIP is available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, enabling a customer to instantly transfer funds from their own account to a beneficiary in another bank at any time of day or night, using the Internet. Restricting it to banking hours (like NEFT's cycle-based processing), requiring a branch visit, or limiting it to government revenue collection all misstate NIP's defining always-on, self-service nature.

questionBank.q: A customer applying for NIP is given a User ID, a User Name, and a Token before they can begin a transfer. What is the purpose of this issuance step in NIP Processing?
opts: It registers the customer for a Mobile Money account instead
It authenticates the remitter before they can access the Internet Platform and initiate a transfer
It replaces the need for the beneficiary's account number
It automatically enrolls the customer in Bulk NEFT
questionBank.exp: The Token, User ID, and User Name are issued to authenticate the remitter, who then accesses the bank's Internet Platform, enters the Token, and proceeds to select Instant Payment and enter the beneficiary's details. This isn't a Mobile Money registration, doesn't replace entering the beneficiary's account number (which is still required), and has nothing to do with Bulk NEFT enrollment.

questionBank.q: NAPS (NIBSS Automated Payment System) resulted from a strategic alliance between NIBSS and which entity, and commenced full operations on what date?
opts: Interswitch, commencing March 2004
System-Specs Limited, commencing February 2, 2015
CSCS, commencing September 4, 2014
Western Union, commencing April 1, 2021
questionBank.exp: NAPS is a product of a strategic alliance between NIBSS and System-Specs Limited, commencing full operations on Monday, February 2, 2015. Interswitch and CSCS are institutions relying on NIBSS rather than NAPS's alliance partner, Western Union is an unrelated foreign FT system, and each listed date belongs to a different milestone entirely (NEFT's 2004 launch and RTGS-on-SWIFT's 2014 date, respectively).

questionBank.q: A customer wants to use their bank's own dedicated Instant Payment System to withdraw physical cash from their account. Is this possible under the system as described?
opts: Yes, cash withdrawal is one of its core functions
No — cash and cheque deposit/withdrawal are excluded
Yes, but only up to a fixed daily cash limit
No, the system is restricted to bill payments only
questionBank.exp: The customer can use the bank's own dedicated Instant Payment device to enjoy more services on the account except the deposit and withdrawal of cash and cheques — this exclusion is explicit. Claiming cash withdrawal is a core function, allowing it up to a daily limit, or restricting the whole system to bill payments only all misstate this specific carve-out.

questionBank.q: A Mobile Money remitter sends funds to a beneficiary who does not have a Mobile Money account of their own. How does the beneficiary receive and claim these funds?
opts: The funds are automatically forfeited back to the remitter after 24 hours
The beneficiary gets a voucher and code to claim funds via an agent
The beneficiary must first open a Mobile Money account before any funds can be sent
The funds are converted automatically into airtime for the beneficiary's network
questionBank.exp: Where the beneficiary has no mobile account, they receive an electronic voucher on their phone, and the remitter also gives them a code they can use to claim the funds from the bank or any of its agents.
