questionBank.q: A bank's IT staff member exploits their system knowledge to transfer funds for personal gain. Which Fraud Feature does this illustrate?
opts: Breach of confidence
Sharp practices
Deprivation
Impropriety
questionBank.exp: Sharp practices is defined as the wrong use of knowledge or skill to gain undue advantage, with an IT staff member exploiting system knowledge for personal fund transfers given as the exact example. Breach of confidence concerns disappointing the trust placed in someone (like an account officer misappropriating deposits), Deprivation concerns direct theft, and Impropriety concerns abuse of office — none match this knowledge-exploitation scenario.

questionBank.q: A branch manager uses the bank's official pool car for personal purposes. Which Fraud Feature does this illustrate?
opts: Sharp practices
Impropriety
Deception
Deprivation
questionBank.exp: Impropriety is defined as abuse of office or betrayal of confidence by trusted top officials, with a branch manager using the bank's pool car for personal purposes given as the exact example. Sharp practices concerns misusing technical knowledge, Deception concerns false pretenses to obtain something, and Deprivation concerns direct theft — none match this specific abuse-of-office example.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed among the Fraudulent Practices in Banks, involving intentionally delayed or manipulated posting of transactions?
opts: Fictitious loan facilities
Dry postings
Impersonation / identity theft
Suppression of cash/cheque
questionBank.exp: Dry postings is explicitly listed among the Fraudulent Practices in Banks. Fictitious loan facilities, impersonation/identity theft, and suppression of cash/cheque are all separate practices also listed in this same section, but they describe different fraudulent mechanisms, not delayed/manipulated posting specifically.

questionBank.q: A teller deliberately withholds recording a customer's cash deposit or cheque lodgment from the books. Which listed Fraudulent Practice in Banks does this describe?
opts: Fraudulent liquidation of fixed deposits
Suppression of cash/cheque
Dry postings
Failure of integrity test
questionBank.exp: Suppression of cash/cheque is the specific listed practice matching deliberate non-recording of a cash deposit or cheque lodgment. Fraudulent liquidation of fixed deposits concerns unauthorized closure of term deposits, Dry postings concerns a different kind of posting manipulation, and Failure of integrity test concerns a staff vetting outcome — none match withholding a deposit from the books.

questionBank.q: The Fraud Triangle theory, explaining why workers decide to commit workplace fraud, was propounded by which scholars?
opts: Milton Friedman and Adam Smith
Donald R. Cressey and Edwin Sutherland
Max Weber and Karl Marx
Peter Drucker and Michael Porter
questionBank.exp: The Fraud Triangle theory was propounded by Donald R. Cressey and Edwin Sutherland, explaining the reasoning behind a worker's decision to commit workplace fraud. Friedman/Smith, Weber/Marx, and Drucker/Porter are all real scholars associated with entirely different fields (economics, sociology, and management theory respectively), not the Fraud Triangle.

questionBank.q: Under the Fraud Triangle, an employee facing peer group pressure feels a motive to commit and conceal fraud. Which element of the triangle does this represent?
opts: Rationalization
Pressure
Opportunity
Deprivation
questionBank.exp: Pressure is specifically defined as peer group pressure that motivates someone to commit and conceal fraud. Rationalization concerns justifying the action after the fact, Opportunity concerns weak controls enabling the act, and Deprivation is actually a separate Fraud Feature (from section 9.3), not a Fraud Triangle element at all.

questionBank.q: A branch has weak segregation of duties, allowing a single staff member to both initiate and approve transactions. Under the Fraud Triangle, which element does this weakness create?
opts: Pressure
Opportunity
Rationalization
Breach of confidence
questionBank.exp: Opportunity is specifically defined as being created by weak controls that provide the chance for a person to commit fraud — matching this exact scenario of poor segregation of duties. Pressure concerns external motivating stress, Rationalization concerns post-hoc justification, and Breach of confidence is a Fraud Feature rather than a Fraud Triangle element.

questionBank.q: An employee who diverted funds tells themselves "I was only borrowing the money" to feel at ease with their actions. Which Fraud Triangle element does this illustrate?
opts: Opportunity
Rationalization
Pressure
Sharp practices
questionBank.exp: Rationalization refers to justifying unethical behavior as something other than criminal activity, and "I was only borrowing the money" is one of Cressey's specific listed examples of this justification. Opportunity concerns weak controls rather than self-justification, Pressure concerns the initial motivating stress, and Sharp practices is a separate Fraud Feature, not a Fraud Triangle element.

questionBank.q: According to the module, approximately what percentage of all fraud cases have been influenced by financial pressure resulting from personal, employment, or external stress?
questionBank.exp: About 95% of all cases of fraud have been influenced by financial pressure resulting from personal, employment stress, and external pressure — a strikingly high figure the module specifically calls out. 25%, 50%, and 75% all significantly understate this stated proportion.

questionBank.q: Which point of the Fraud Triangle can internal control procedures particularly diminish, according to the module?
opts: Pressure
Opportunity
Rationalization
All three points equally and by the same mechanism
questionBank.exp: Internal control procedures can particularly diminish the "Opportunity" point of the Fraud Triangle, since opportunity is created specifically by ineffective control or governance systems. Pressure stems from personal/external stress that controls don't directly address, Rationalization is a psychological justification process, and claiming all three are diminished equally by the same mechanism overstates what internal controls specifically target.

questionBank.q: Under the Bank Fraud Types by Department table, which fraud-prone activity is listed specifically under Cash & Teller?
opts: Cheque Kiting
Vault Manipulation
Phishing
Fictitious loan facilities
questionBank.exp: Vault Manipulation is listed specifically under the Cash & Teller department's fraud-prone activities, alongside cash shortage, forged instruments, cash movements crime, theft of valuable items, and cash counterfeit. Cheque Kiting is listed instead under Bank Clearing Operations, Phishing under Electronic Banking, and Fictitious loan facilities relates to Credit/Marketing — each a different department's activity.

questionBank.q: An employee at the Customer Service unit approves an account opening despite missing documentation, exploiting a policy exception meant for genuine delays. Which listed fraud-prone activity under Customer Service does this match?
opts: Dormant Account
Abuse of Waivers/Deferral
Fake References
Opening account for unknown clients
questionBank.exp: Abuse of Waivers/Deferral is the specific listed Customer Service fraud-prone activity matching exploitation of a documentation exception process. Dormant Account, Fake References, and Opening account for unknown clients are all separate listed activities under the same department, describing different specific vulnerabilities.

questionBank.q: A Funds Transfer staff member fabricates the authentication code used to verify a transfer instruction between correspondent banks. Which listed fraud-prone activity does this match?
opts: Use of stolen cheque or draft
Forged Test Codes/messages
Exposure of client's information
Fraudulent transfer
questionBank.exp: Forged Test Codes/messages is the specific listed Funds Transfer fraud-prone activity matching fabrication of authentication codes used between correspondent banks. Use of stolen cheque/draft, Exposure of client's information, and Fraudulent transfer are all separate listed activities under the same department, each describing a distinct vulnerability.

questionBank.q: A customer deposits a cheque into one account and withdraws against it before it has actually cleared, cycling funds between accounts to create artificial available balances. Which listed Bank Clearing Operations fraud-prone activity does this describe?
opts: Payment of incomplete cheques
Cheque Kiting
Suppression of instruments
Collusion with Clearing Officers
questionBank.exp: Cheque Kiting is the specific listed Bank Clearing Operations activity matching this exact cycling-of-uncleared-funds scheme. Payment of incomplete cheques, Suppression of instruments, and Collusion with Clearing Officers are separate listed activities under the same department, describing different clearing-related vulnerabilities.

questionBank.q: An IT department staff member is found to have access to customer data far beyond what their role requires, with no restriction in place. Which listed IT fraud-prone activity does this describe?
opts: Manipulation of the programs by IT staff members
Unrestricted access to database
Data corruption for unlawful motive
Cyber Attacks
questionBank.exp: Unrestricted access to database is the specific listed IT fraud-prone activity matching excessive, unrestricted data access. Manipulation of programs, Data corruption, and Cyber Attacks are separate listed IT activities describing different specific vulnerabilities, not the access-scope issue this scenario describes.

questionBank.q: Two treasury dealers work together to manipulate a deal's terms for their mutual personal benefit, without the bank's knowledge. Which listed Treasury/TROPS fraud-prone activity does this match?
opts: Creating fictitious deposit account
Collusion between treasury dealers
Unauthorized fund placement at the branch
Collusion with a depositor to defraud the bank
questionBank.exp: Collusion between treasury dealers is the specific listed Treasury/TROPS fraud-prone activity matching this exact scenario of two dealers conspiring together. Creating a fictitious deposit account, Unauthorized fund placement, and Collusion with a depositor are separate listed activities under the same department, each involving a different party or mechanism.

questionBank.q: A relationship manager secures approval for a loan to a business that does not actually exist, exposing the bank to potential failure. Which listed Credit/Marketing fraud-prone activity does this match?
opts: Manipulation of customers account
Getting approval to book fictitious loans that may lead to bank failure
Manipulation of rates
Collusion with customers to defraud the bank
questionBank.exp: Getting approval to book fictitious loans that may lead to bank failure is the specific listed Credit/Marketing activity matching this exact scenario of a loan to a non-existent business. Manipulation of customers' accounts, Manipulation of rates, and Collusion with customers are separate listed activities under the same department, each describing a different fraud mechanism.

questionBank.q: A fraudster uses a small device fitted to an ATM's card slot to copy a customer's card data as they insert it. Which listed Electronic Banking fraud-prone activity does this match?
opts: Phishing
Skimming
Social Engineering
Identity Theft/Account Take-Over
questionBank.exp: Skimming is the specific listed Electronic Banking activity matching card-data copying via a device fitted to a card reader. Phishing instead involves deceptive emails or messages, Social Engineering involves manipulating people directly, and Identity Theft/Account Take-Over describes a broader outcome rather than this specific card-cloning technique — though skimming can lead to it.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed among the reasons banks are vulnerable to fraud, relating to the sheer scale of what banks hold?
opts: Banks are legally required to disclose all customer balances publicly
Banks hold vast amounts of money and assets, making them attractive targets
Banks operate with no regulatory oversight whatsoever
Banks employ fewer staff than most other industries
questionBank.exp: Banks holding vast amounts of money and assets, making them attractive targets for criminals seeking financial gain, is explicitly listed as a vulnerability reason. Public disclosure of balances, an absence of regulatory oversight, and lower staffing than other industries are not accurate claims and are not among the listed vulnerability reasons.

questionBank.q: A bank partners with a third-party fintech vendor whose security measures turn out to be inadequate. Which listed vulnerability reason does this exposure reflect?
opts: Complexity of banking products and processes
Interoperability of banks and third-party vendors/service providers, which may give rise to security vulnerabilities
Increasing shift in digital banking technology
Employees having access to sensitive information
questionBank.exp: Interoperability of banks and third-party vendors and service providers is explicitly listed as a vulnerability reason, specifically noting that inadequate partner security measures may give rise to vulnerabilities — matching this exact scenario. Product/process complexity, the digital shift generally, and employee access are all separate listed vulnerability reasons, not the third-party-partner-specific one this scenario illustrates.

questionBank.q: Beyond direct income loss, which of the following is explicitly listed among the Effects/Impact of Fraud on a bank?
opts: Increased shareholder dividends
Loss of Tax Revenue to Government
Improved regulatory relationships
Reduced need for internal audit
questionBank.exp: Loss of Tax Revenue to Government is explicitly listed among the Effects/Impact of Fraud, alongside loss of confidence by shareholders, loss of patronage by customers, shock and trauma, regulatory surveillance, investigations, image problems, and contagion risk. Increased dividends, improved regulator relationships, and reduced need for audit all contradict the negative impacts actually listed.

questionBank.q: The module notes that the effects of fraud "could be contagious." What does this specific listed effect suggest about fraud within an organization?
opts: That fraud is a communicable disease affecting bank staff physically
That one instance or culture of fraud can spread to affect other parts of the organization or normalize further fraudulent behavior
That fraud losses are always immediately covered by deposit insurance
That fraud effects are limited strictly to the department where it occurred
questionBank.exp: Listing "could be contagious" as an effect points to the risk that fraud spreads or normalizes across an organization, rather than staying contained — consistent with the module's broader emphasis on culture, controls, and oversight. It is not a literal physical illness claim, doesn't imply automatic insurance coverage of losses, and directly contradicts the idea that effects stay confined to one department.

questionBank.q: Fraud Risk Management Strategies are grouped into three categories based on timing relative to the fraud event. What are these three categories?
opts: Financial, Operational, and Reputational
Preventive, Detective, and Corrective
Internal, External, and Regulatory
Cash, Credit, and Treasury-based
questionBank.exp: The three categories are Preventive (proactive measures to stop fraud from occurring), Detective (mechanisms to identify fraud when it occurs), and Corrective (strategies to mitigate impact and prevent recurrence). Financial/Operational/Reputational, Internal/External/Regulatory, and Cash/Credit/Treasury-based are not the actual three-category framework the module uses for fraud risk management strategies.

questionBank.q: A bank implements segregation of duties, authorization procedures, and access controls after conducting a risk assessment to identify system vulnerabilities. Which Fraud Risk Management category does this activity fall under?
opts: Fraud Detection
Fraud Prevention, specifically Controls Implementation
Fraud Correction
Fraud Triangle Rationalization
questionBank.exp: This matches Fraud Prevention's Controls Implementation component specifically — implementing preventive controls such as segregation of duties, authorization procedures, and access controls based on a prior risk assessment. Fraud Detection concerns identifying fraud once it's already occurring, Fraud Correction concerns responding after the fact, and Rationalization is a Fraud Triangle element, not a risk management strategy category.

questionBank.q: A bank deploys machine learning algorithms and anomaly detection software to sift through large transaction volumes and flag potential fraud indicators in near-real-time. Which Fraud Risk Management component does this describe?
opts: Fraud Prevention's Employee Awareness component
Fraud Detection's Technology Utilization component
Fraud Correction's Legal & Disciplinary Actions component
Fraud Correction's Enhancement of Controls component
questionBank.exp: This matches Fraud Detection's Technology Utilization component — employing data analytics, machine learning, AI, and anomaly detection software to identify potential fraud indicators, operating in real-time or near-real-time. Employee Awareness concerns training rather than technology, and both listed Fraud Correction components concern reactive responses after fraud has already been identified and investigated, not the identification process itself.

questionBank.q: After confirming that fraud has occurred, a bank conducts a thorough investigation to determine its scope and perpetrators, then pursues recovery of losses and strengthens controls to prevent recurrence. Which Fraud Risk Management component does this match?
opts: Fraud Prevention's Risk Assessment component
Fraud Correction's Investigation & Remediation component
Fraud Detection's Real-time Monitoring component
Fraud Prevention's Digital Security component
questionBank.exp: This matches Fraud Correction's Investigation & Remediation component — conducting thorough investigations upon detection of fraud, then recovering losses, sanctioning wrongdoers, and strengthening controls. Risk Assessment and Digital Security are both proactive Prevention components applied before fraud occurs, and Real-time Monitoring is a Detection component focused on identifying fraud as it happens, not the reactive investigation-and-remediation process this scenario describes.

questionBank.q: A bank fails to obtain the name of a customer's employer during staff account opening. Which listed Act of Negligence does this represent?
opts: Failure to see the original certificate of registration
Failure to obtain the customer's employer's name at staff account opening
Failure to attend to account opening formalities
Failure to enquire into an unusual collection's circumstances
questionBank.exp: This is listed as its own distinct Act of Negligence — failure to obtain the customer's employer's name specifically during staff account opening. Failure to see the registration certificate, general account-opening formalities, and failure to enquire into unusual collections are each separate, distinctly worded items on the same list, not this one.

questionBank.q: A government agency applies to open a Public Sector account. Beyond standard identification, which specific document must be provided to establish the institution's legal existence?
opts: A Partnership Agreement between partners
A copy of the Gazette or Decree establishing it
A Trust Deed for the institution
A Certificate of Registration of Business Name
questionBank.exp: Public Sector account opening specifically requires a copy of the Gazette/Decree establishing the institution, alongside a letter of authorisation from the supervising ministry and a letter appointing signatories signed by officers named in the Gazette. A Partnership Agreement, Trust Deed, and Business Name registration are documentation requirements for other account categories (partnerships, NGOs, and clubs respectively), not Public Sector accounts.

questionBank.q: At the start of the day, a teller's cash allocation is posted from the vault into the teller's position using a teller transfer slip. What is this specific procedure called?
opts: Vault-out registration
Cashing-in
Departmental proof
Cash sweep
questionBank.exp: This exact procedure — posting the cash allocation into the teller's position via the teller transfer slip — is specifically named "cashing-in." Vault-out registration isn't the term used in this procedure, departmental proof is an end-of-day reconciliation document, and cash sweep is a vault-deposit source from external collection points, not this beginning-of-day allocation step.

questionBank.q: What was the initial maximum value fixed by the CBN for a single cheque processed through the clearing system?
opts: N5 million
N10 million
N20 million
N50 million
questionBank.exp: The initial limit fixed by the CBN is N10 million, though the manual notes this can change later. N5 million understates the figure, while N20 million and N50 million both overstate it.

questionBank.q: The Commencement of the Nigerian Uniform Bank Account Number (NUBAN) resulted from the conclusion of which CBN-driven assignment?
opts: The Dishonoured Cheques Act review process
The PSV2020 infrastructure assignment
The Special Caution Notice reform
The eCCI project
questionBank.exp: NUBAN's commencement, alongside updating the Nigerian Bankers Clearing House Rules, was one of the conclusions of the PSV2020-related assignment to modernize Nigeria's Automated Clearing House infrastructure. The Dishonoured Cheques Act review, Special Caution Notice reform, and eCCI project are all real but separate initiatives covered elsewhere in the course, not the one that produced NUBAN.

questionBank.q: CBN T24, now known as DEPO X, is an integral part of RTGS offering which range of services?
opts: Only FX settlement between correspondent banks
Depository, trading, transfer, settlement, and clearing, real-time gross
Only interbank transfer messaging
Only Treasury Bills auction processing
questionBank.exp: DEPO X (formerly CBN T24) offers a range of services including depository, trading, transfer of money and securities, settlement, and clearing, on a real-time and gross basis. Foreign currency settlement between correspondent banks is SWIFT's role instead, interbank funds transfer messaging describes CIFTS/NISS, and Treasury Bills auction processing alone understates DEPO X's actual range of services.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as a fraud-prone activity specifically under the Financial Control/General Admin department?
opts: Collusion between treasury dealers
Abuse of operating expenses
Vault manipulation
Forged test codes/messages
questionBank.exp: Abuse of operating expenses (alongside abuse of capital expenses) is listed specifically under the Financial Control/General Admin department's fraud-prone activities. Collusion between treasury dealers belongs to Treasury/TROPS, vault manipulation to Cash & Teller, and forged test codes to Funds Transfer — each a different department's listed activity.
